Lateral group transfer question: In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

Edit: Looking through past posts I see I have broached this issue before! See https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1342845/article/35597336#35597336 where no conclusion was reached :)

ground_truth_answer:
In the General Vol 21 Number 1 scenario A series replay, on turn 5 the American plays a sideways movement card on his group C "as a Lateral Group Transfer". But given the German player only has groups at identity chit A and B isn't this illegal? Rule 17.7 first sentence says "... directly opposite an opposing group ..."

No, it says "A group capable of movement can change its group identity and thereby its position directly opposing an enemy group...."  All it is saying if you move group from B to C, the directly opposing group would now be C--if it exists.  If the opponent  does not have a Group C, then there would be no directly opposing group to your Group C.  (Just like there would be if each side set up with a different number of groups at start.)

It is not stating a requirement, but a change of status of "directly opposing" groups.

The rule states the player announces the intention to perform a lateral group transfer so presumably if the player doesn't make the announcement at the time of playing the movement card sideways he can't subsequently do so on a future turn (using that same played movement card) even if the necessary conditions still exist to make such a move? 

Correct, if the intention to change a group's ID is not made when playing the movement cards, when group enters terrain, the same Group ID remains.  Very common if you want to get into better terrain.

Where a game is played without aid of voice or text chat I guess you might agree that a lateral group transfer announcement was accompanied by putting down the new group identity chit in the adjacent column and taken away if the attempt failed.

A common technique in ftf play is to place the new ID on the Movement card until new terrain is accepted or rejected (which would cancel the transfer).

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

I would say no per errata on Rule 5:  Movement cards not played directly to the discard pile cannot voluntarily be cancelled.  (Just like you can't rotate a Movement card from advancing to sideways because you change your mind about advancing.)

Edit: Looking through past posts I see I have broached this issue before! See https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1342845/article/35597336#35597336 where no conclusion was reached :)

No big deal, that thread started 11 years ago and you added your question 5 years after that.

Prisoners/guarding (32): Taking a deep dive into rules I never see used in the games I've played of UF.  

From a re-formatted rule book that embeds the Q/A.  

32.12 & 16.42 By capturing a man and bringing him into a group, and
then stopping in suitable terrain, does the attacker satisfy the Relative
Range 5 requirement of the Victory Conditions, if, in so doing, it
eliminates the only Relative Range 5 enemy group?
A. Yes. Note, this rule is in effect to prevent a player from routing men
to avoid victory by the opponent.

---

I don't understand the answer.  Players can't rout men of their own volition that I know of.  I could see someone voluntarily panic one of their PCs to eliminate a RR5 situation.  Is that what it's talking about?
---

Prisoners, once taken, are placed
beneath the card of any one man in the capturing
group of the capturing player's choice. That man
may be pinned, wounded, or even unarmed but he
may not be the designated assistant crewman for any weapon.

---

It's not "that man may NOT be pinned"  Pinned PCs can actually do something?  The only thing is guarding?

--

If the designated assistant crewman is the only possible choice...

--

How is that possible?  Who is he crewing for if he's the only choice?

--

A player may change guards automatically as the sole Action of a group for that turn provided
the new guard is not currently pinned.

--

The 2nd paragraph says yes for pinned PCs as guards and the last says no.  I see there's a, very, slight difference in the initiation of the guard duty between the two but I don't see the point.

This is a rare situation.  It would only matter in a rear guard action scenarios ("X unpinmed men at RR5 (not Range Chit 4/5)") with all men in the group are pinned.

Prisoners, in general, are often forgotten about--I saw it once or twice in CC to get 5VP in a city fight.

---

I don't understand the answer.  Players can't rout men of their own volition that I know of.  I could see someone voluntarily panic one of their PCs to eliminate a RR5 situation.  Is that what it's talking about?

Yes.  You cannot simply rout a man.   You can voluntarily panic a pinned man. but there would be chance he dies rather than routs/captured at RR5.  Nor can you voluntarily rout unpinned men.

It is an attempt to prevent a spoil sport play when an Attacker reaches RR5 and only needs to reach good terrain or rally pinned men and the Defender voluntarily panics to eliminate that group.  At least the man could be captured (if he didn't KIA) preserving the justified win.  But obviously if he did KIA. this rule doesn't fix the problem.

At least it is VERY unlikely to come up:  It would be a late game desperation move by the defender who otherwise is not close to breaking his squad in Scenarios D or Q.

Prisoners, once taken, are placed
beneath the card of any one man in the capturing
group of the capturing player's choice. That man
may be pinned, wounded, or even unarmed but he
may not be the designated assistant crewman for any weapon.

---

It's not "that man may NOT be pinned"  Pinned PCs can actually do something?  The only thing is guarding?

Yes, that is what it says--even though it says should the guard be eliminated, his prisoners must be reassigned to an unpinned man.  (I have a feeling Courtney Allen and Don Greenwood may have been hemming and hawing on this rule.)

--

If the designated assistant crewman is the only possible choice...

--

How is that possible?  Who is he crewing for if he's the only choice?

Good, then this rule would NEVER come up!  (See what I wrote above!)

--

A player may change guards automatically as the sole Action of a group for that turn provided
the new guard is not currently pinned.

--

The 2nd paragraph says yes for pinned PCs as guards and the last says no.  I see there's a, very, slight difference in the initiation of the guard duty between the two but I don't see the point.  

Also, per errata, unpinned man must be in the capturing group in order to capture during a rout.

If you want to play with a house rule that says "Pinned men cannot be assigned to guard prisoners, but they can retain that role if later pinned", I don't think most opponents would object.  And that seems to fix the holes you found. (re: crewman and reassignment.)

As I said above, prisoners do not come up frequently:
-  You have get groups at RR5, which happens infrequently in the first place.
-  The players in that situation are usually more concerned with CC to eliminate the group or winning the scenario.
-  And unless the scenario is going to be determined by victory points (Only can happen in Scenarios A, B, G, J, M,  N.), the attacker would rather not take a prisoner at all--if only to avoid fp/To Hit penalties.  And rule 32.12 allows the "capturing" player to not take a prisoner if otherwise able, leaving the enemy man to rout instead.

AFV questions (stun effect, etc.): Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.
title: AFV questions (stun effect, etc.)
raw_question:
Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.
ground_truth_answer:
Couple of things - about getting AFVs to button up, one way for infantry to reduce the threat of an AFV is to fire at it with small arms, hoping to get a hit equal to or higher than its Morale value, which forces it to button up.  This is covered by 28.3:

An AFV card has two Armor defense values printed on each side of the card plus a Morale and CE Defense value on the front of the card. The Armor and Flank defense values represent the armored defense strength and is listed on both sides of the card; only attacks using solely boxed firepower or boxed "Effect Numbers" apply to this value. The MORALE and CE values are affected only by unboxed attack values.

This is how mortars can attack AFVs (and they have a small chance of damaging the vehicle as well [26.5]).  AT guns have the choice of firing AP - the process the OP referred to in his second question, which attacks the Armor/Flank values - or HE, which attacks the Morale value as above.  The HE attack is only possible, of course, when the vehicle is CE, or in the case of an OT vehicle if it is not already Pinned (except for one or two really weedy AFVs like the British Bren Carrier, which has a Panic value and can thus be attacked when Pinned).

And moving on to the OPs second question, you were right to feel that there should be a random element is resolving an AP hit - and there is!  25.4 says:

Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.)  The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5]. 

So the Hit process establishes first whether a hit has been obtained, and secondly how damaging it is: for HE, the RNC on the To Hit card is used (provided a 0 would have hit, reflecting how close the HE round actually landed), and for AP a hit is a hit, but the RR is added to reflect increased penetration at closer ranges.  This gives you the base hit strength; then, in both cases, you draw an RNC for each target.  Firing at an AFV, of course, there is only one target, but you still draw an RNC.

So, a Panther (s7,i8,k9) rumbles up to RR4 to a plucky British 6-pdr (FE 3).  If the AT gun gets a hit, its base Hit Strength will be 3+4=7, and then it hopes the RNC will be at least 0, and preferably a black 2 or better to get a kill.

Don't forget, also, that unlike small arms and HE fire against an AFV, terrain does affect the resolution.  So if the AFV is in Brush, the Hit Strength is reduced by 1.  I suppose this reflects the possibility of the round being deflected or slowed by intervening obstacles.

Hope all that helps!  Oh, and Snipers are good, too.

The 17.4 section only refers to Flanking Fire.  It's specifying that specific rule.  Not the Natural one as far as I can tell.  

FF is lost when the flanking group plays a movement but that would be an odd condition for NFF since it wouldn't necessarily break the conditions needed for NFF. title: Rules don't explicitly tell you when you lose Natural Flanking Fire?
raw_question:
I imagine it's as simple as you are no longer in the conditions for it and therefore don't have it.  The 17.4 section only refers to Flanking Fire.  It's specifying that specific rule.  Not the Natural one as far as I can tell.

Removing wire and failing to Ford a stream would make you lose NFF?  But how would one regain NFF as you're still in the exact same conditions to qualify for it?  But... the condition for NFF is moving forward to RR4 (chits 6) from RR5.  That seems to be it.  Moving forward.  So stopping at RR4 (6 on chits) you lose it as you no longer are moving? I know over thinking it but...
ground_truth_answer:
Flanking is a complicated rule.

Gaining Natural Flanking is a result of moving from RR5 to "RR6" per 17.3.. (I prefer "RR6" to "RR4 but behind the target group".)

Losing any form of Flanking occurs under 17.4X, specifically:
-  Flanking group has a movement or Wire played on it.  (but not Terrain--needed to get doubled FP without 1/2FP for moving.)
-  Flanked group has terrain, even if rejected.
-  Flanked group has a Movement played on it, even temporarily to remove Wire or failed Ford attempt.
-  Front group eliminated or changes ID chit/completes a lateral group "transfer".

Gaining flanking (either naturally or via a Flank card) places a Flank Fire chit.  Losing Flanking removes the Flank Fire chit.  The presence of the ***chit*** determines doubled FP for flanking.

Once, natural flanking is lost  it would be difficult to regain. (retreat to RR5 and advance back to RR6) But, when in a natural Flanking position (i.e. RR6) (whether Flanking was lost or not), that group can Encircle on a later turn (if the Front group is at RR2 to the Flanked group), by playing a sideways Movement cards on the Flanking group.

And always double/halve all FP before rounding down.

You are correct, the attacker man in CC will be an infiltrator.  As pointed out above, a man in the defending group could be infiltrating the attacking group (or a different attacking group also at RR5), and rule covers those situations.  

Note, it is more difficult to infiltrate from a group which has been infiltrated by their opponent (20.39)

There might be others, but what pops to mind is 20.9 Berserk, and (although it was likely not considered when 20.73 was written), 45.4 BANZAI.

Keeping infiltration status would not apply to Banzai or Berserk, because in neither case is the man an infiltrator.  (20.91, 45.422)

query:
Killed SL: If your SL is killed or panics, you draw one less card "during that game turn". So if my opponent kills it during his turn (which I would expected is the most frequent case), the ASL will take over during my turn and I will not be penalized, right?

I just think it's weird that such a dramatic death does not entail a one-shot penalty.
title: Killed SL
raw_question:
If your SL is killed or panics, you draw one less card "during that game turn". So if my opponent kills it during his turn (which I would expected is the most frequent case), the ASL will take over during my turn and I will not be penalized, right?

I just think it's weird that such a dramatic death does not entail a one-shot penalty.
ground_truth_answer:
Unfortunately, I find no definition for Game Turn vs Player Turn, but the implication here is that 1 Game Turn = 2 consecutive Player Turns. Also, as you note, it would be weird if there was no penalty...so inflict the penalty.

4. SEQUENCE OF PLAY
4.1 The game begins with the player specified by the scenario taking his
play first. [In Design Your Own (henceforth referred to as DYO) scenarios
the player having spent less point on the construction of his force gets to
move first with ties resolved by RNC draw.] When he is finished, the
opposing player takes his turn. Player turns are then alternated until one
of the participants achieves his Victory Conditions as required by the
scenario in play or the Time Limit expires.

15.2 Should a player's SL be pinned at the end of his turn, or have just
been removed by a KIA or PANIC result during that game turn, that player
may only draw enough cards to restore the number of cards in his hand
[4.5] to one less than the number he is usually allotted.

P.S. We blew the dust off this recently to have two of us teach two others, and I noticed players (we two "veterans" included) had trouble remembering to short the hand by a card due to 15.2, so I had us park a regular card deck's JOKER under each SL to help us remember. If the SL was "15.2-ed", then that Joker was picked up into the SL-possessor's hand as a reminder that it was causing hand capacity problems. The card would get parked under the ASL if required. An additional bonus was that it also made it easier for the opponent to spot the SL's group, speeding the game up slightly during targetting choices.

Minefield attacks are played on the same group resulting in the

The point of the rule is you have only have the right to retarget a sniper or Minefield if it's target group ends up empty before resolution.  You cannot do that with other active discards (Terrain, Wire)

title: Clarification on split action cards and nationality markings
raw_question:
Re-reading the rules, I noticed something that I think I "learned" incorrectly years ago, when there's two possible actions on a split action card.  The image serves to illustrate my question.   

Q:   Do nationality markings refer to everything on that side of the card?    In particular, when nationality markings are along the side of the card where it says Radio.  

The card on the left I had long interpreted to mean any nation could use it as a Rally card, but only the American or Russian player could use it for the Radio.  But re-reading the rules, now I think that only the American or Russian can use the card at all, for either Rally or Radio.

ground_truth_answer:
If the card is a Split Action card with RADIO, then only the nationalities indicated on that side can use the card as RADIO or RALLY (because all RADIO cards are paired with rallies).

If the card is NOT  a split action card, but has nationality indicators next to RADIO, any nationality can use the card to Rally, but only the indicated nationalities can use the RADIO.

Also of course, Japanese use Russian Split Action, French use German and British use either German or American except for a RADIO which must be both German AND American.  Italian use no Split Actions (unless elite).

query:
Does a group directly opposite to a Banzai declaration, that decreases its range chit, permit Banzai cancellation?: Hello everyone,

Given this section of rule 45.43:
"The Japanese player has the option to cancel a 
Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no 
longer directly opposite or adjacent), "

Situation: A group declares Banzai on a directly opposite group at RR 1. The target group of the Banzai retrograde moves and decreases its range chit from 1 to 0.
Does the Banzai group have the option to cancel the Banzai? 

I am not sure if the "out of range" and parenthetical section applies to both parts of the "or"

Thanks,

John
title: Does a group directly opposite to a Banzai declaration, that decreases its range chit, permit Banzai cancellation?
raw_question:
Hello everyone,

Given this section of rule 45.43:
"The Japanese player has the option to cancel a 
Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no 
longer directly opposite or adjacent), "

Situation: A group declares Banzai on a directly opposite group at RR 1. The target group of the Banzai retrograde moves and decreases its range chit from 1 to 0.
Does the Banzai group have the option to cancel the Banzai? 

I am not sure if the "out of range" and parenthetical section applies to both parts of the "or"

Thanks,

John
ground_truth_answer:
No.  Simply retreating does not allow the Japanese to cancel Banzai.  But retreating (or moving laterally or having another group moving) to a positon where Banzai could not have been declared.  The "out of range" wording is really terrible.

Moving laterally is easy to explain.  Japanese Group A declares Banzai on American Group B.  Then the targetted American Group moves laterally moves to C--then the targeted group is now "out of range" (i.e. no longer directly opposite or adjacent.) so now the Japanese could cancel the Banzai.

As for retreating causing a Banzai group to be no longer eligible to be Banzaied, you have to check the errata.
Per the errata, 45.4 should have inserted after the third sentence, "However, Banzai may not be declared against an enemy group that is blocked at the time Banzai is declared."  
 It gives an example (modified slightly to make better example for this question).

AM:  A(3)  B(2)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)
The Japanese player cannot have Group A declare Banzai against American Group B, because direct movement of Japan A to American B to RR5 is not possible since it is blocked by American A.

What happens if a targetted group retreats into a blocked position, like this:

AM:  A(3)  B(3)
JP:  A(0)  B(0)

Japan A declares Banzai on American B, then Anerican B retreats to RC 2 and is now in a blocked position (like above).  Now, the Japanese Group A can cancel the Banzai, because now Banzaiing Japan group A is blocked from targetted American Group B by American Group A.

What happens if American A moves forward to RC4 after Japan A declared Banzai on American B in this position.  The same thing!  Banzai Japan A is blocked from tragetted American B by American A.

The sentence from Rule 45.43 quoted in the original question is incomplete.  In full it reads:
The Japanese player has the option to cancel a Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent),  or if another enemy moves in such a way as to block the access of the Banzai group to the declared target.

The missing text covers this third situation.

The Japanese are allowed to cancel a Banzai only if a position arises where it would not be legal to declare it.  This also prevents a Banzaiing group from attacking a different enemy group than the one it is targetting (which never mentioned in the rules or errata--given the blocking rules, obviously is not allowed.)

Hope this helps.

query: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
title: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
raw_question: Can terrain be discarded on a Lateral Group Transfer?
ground_truth_answer:
Ok. So say it's just one man doing a lateral group transfer leaving a group that is in a building for a group in another building. My opponent drops a stream on my guy. Is he now alone in the stream? Does he become his own group? Is the group that he left now in a stream as well? What's going on here?

You seem to be confusing Lateral Group Transfer with Individual Transfer.  The rules are unnecessarily confusing with calling both very different actions "transfers".

Lateral Group Transfer (17.7) = lateral movement of a group from Group B to Group C (for example).  (This should be called "Lateral Movement".)  This is initiated by playing a Movement card in sideways mode while declaring the Lateral Movement.  (I generally put the new group marker on the movement card).  Prerequisite:  there can be no group ID in the location that you are going to (unless you are switching positions of two groups--which I won't get into here.)  On a later turn, the Transf...I mean Lateral Movement is completed by playing terrain on the group (The Group ID applies only now.)  The Lateral Movement is cancelled if terrain discarded by opponent is rejected or if open ground played under Wire that was played on the Laterally Moving group (as either would remove sideways Movement card.)

Individual Transfer (17.8) is transferring Individual men between groups.  First, the groups must be adjacent and at the same range chit and one or both groups must have an unpinned leader.  Then, one Movement card is played for each transferring man (more than one man can transfer.) and a Transfer chit on the man.  Transfer is completed when the receiving group uses an action to accept the transferring men (which can be placed in any position in their new group).  While transferring, they are "first men" resolved if either group is fired at, do not get any entrenchment TEM and an additional +2 TEM.  If a transferring man is pinned, its Transfer is cancelled and is returned to the sending group.  (During normal individual transfer, terrain cannot be discarded on the transferring man/men.  Both originating/destination groups will have terrain/OG in any  case.)

Group Creation (17.9) done by using Individual Transfer rules:
-  Group ID they are transferring to must be vacant.
-  Two or more men must be transferred at the same time to initiate Group Creation. 
-  If any of these men are pinned in the act of transferring, all transferring men are returned to their original group and Group Creation is cancelled.
-  Completed by playing a terrain card on the new group.  (Errata) If an opponent discards terrain on the new group, it can be accepted (thus completing Group Creation) or rejected.  If rejected, the transfer is cancelled and men returned to original group.

I VERY RARELY attempt group creation.

Hope this helps.

query:
AFV overrun and encirclement......: Just in the middle of playing scenario F , Infantry's Iron Fist.
I have the Soviet T 60 in group C opposite 4 German Infantry in Group C. The T 60 got to RR5 and has done an overrun. Afterwards I played a forward movement card and went through group C to RR4 behind it. Is German group C encircled? There is a Soviet group B.
I understand how the regular infantry encirclement works.
However since the AFV can actually go through an opposite group, unlike infantry, what is the purpose of the AFV going through?
title: AFV overrun and encirclement......
raw_question:
Just in the middle of playing scenario F , Infantry's Iron Fist.
I have the Soviet T 60 in group C opposite 4 German Infantry in Group C. The T 60 got to RR5 and has done an overrun. Afterwards I played a forward movement card and went through group C to RR4 behind it. Is German group C encircled? There is a Soviet group B.
I understand how the regular infantry encirclement works.
However since the AFV can actually go through an opposite group, unlike infantry, what is the purpose of the AFV going through?
ground_truth_answer:
No.  It is not encircled, which per 17.6 requires having a directly opposing group in front of the encircled group no further than RR2 (see 17.613)

Now, AH did not write the rules to cover situations where opposing groups with same ID actually get behind each other, as it so rarely happens (except in Scenario X, Surrounded, which has a special rule covering encirclements--have to be encircled from the same "force".)  So, now that the AFV has passed the target group, that encirclement probably could be obtained by moving the adjacent group at RR4 sideways, since it would fit the regular rules for encirclement in reverse.  (But that way lies madness!)

As for why advance through the enemy after an overrun?  You are not required to, but you might do it to get into position for victory points/conditions.  I'd be more likely to stay at RR5 and fire or overrun again until the enemy group is eliminated.

ground_truth_answer:
I thought i knew this game but maybe i do not. 

Don't worry.  Up Front has some of the worst rules ever.  It is still my favorite wargame.

So If an attack gets the exact number equal to KIA value of an unpinned personality card (lets say an eight), then that card is not KIA is the wound column is equal to printed morale value. 

If the final fire resolution number (i.e. including the RNC for the man) exactly equals the KIA # then you check RPC7w and if RPC7w equals the morale value of the man, the man will be wounded instead of KIA.  This happens whether the target man was pinned or not and he will retain his (un)pinned status.

But also lets say you have a pinned card and attack it is equal to greater than the panic number so you check the rout number and the rnc rout column says it routs  instead fo panic but also the wound column matches the morale, that card does not panic, does not route but instead is wounded. Is that right?

Not quite.  Rule 33.1 Wounds states that wounds "may possibly occur anytime an infantryman **routs** or otherwise be eliminated by a KIA result as a result of an RNC generating a final attack strength exactly equal to the lowest number required for KIA."  This would require a wound check on RPC7 when the pinned man routs as well.

To summarize:
On a pinned man:
- if the Fire Resolution number (FRN) > KIA, the man is dead.  No wound check is made.
-  if the FRN = KIA (usually 9), check for wound
-  if FRN < KIA but >= PANIC, first check RPC0r determine ROUT/KIA.

-  if RPC0r > Rout #, the man likely routs, but check for wound first.
- if RPC0r <= Rout #, the man is KIA. No wound check.

Note, this very rule came up at this year's WBC tournament.  So even experts screw up these rules.

raw_question:

ground_truth_answer:
I've just recently started playing Up Front as a solitaire game. And I realize that weapon malfunction is probably the most contentious rules section. I've looked through the errata and some of the other posts here on this forum, but there's still a case that came up in my play session that I havn't been able to figure out.

Yes.  Malfunction rules are some of the most confusing in the game.  Pretty much you have to follow the errata exclusively.

This is a legacy from Squad Leader's malfunction rules.  Roll the worst natural number and weapon breaks--but only weapons on separate counters were affected--not every rifle which were intrinsic to each squad counter.

19.11 says "If the firing group contains only one firing weapon with usable firepower factors, and a red RNC is drawn to resolve its attack that weapon automatically malfunctions..."

No, it says "Red 6 RNC", though technically that isn't correct.  It should be "Red RNC drawn that causes a malfunction."  This makes a difference with uncrewed machine guns (and Japanese and Italian LMGs) which have a malfunction number of x5-6.

Basically, that sentence is telling you no RPC is needed to determine which weapon broke--because there's only one.  The next clause of that rule states the attack terminates when this happens and no further men in the target group need be resolved.

So, question no. 1: If I have a German group containing only a single personality card:  #4 with a Bolt-Action rifle. If this group fires and the RNC is a red 2, will Pvt. Schumacher's Mauser malfunction automatically?

No, because the rifle breaks on a Red 6.  If it were Red 6, then the rifle would malfunction and it would end the attack.

Question no. 2: If this group instead was a German group consisting of two personality cards: #1 with a Machine Pistol which is assisting crew to #3 with an LMG. And the RNC is a red 2, will the Pfc. Schüssel's MG 34 automatically malfunction?

How many men are  is in this group?  I count three:
1)  a machine Pistol as a crewman for
2)  an LMG
3)  a rifleman

I am going to assume three men for this explanation.  (All unpinned)  I have my reasons.

If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three are considered firing and are subject to malfunction, an RPC(3) is drawn per 19.13 per errata:
-  On a 1, the crewman is affected, no malfunction occurs and the attack continues with -1 to Fire Strength for the remaining men for a momentary belt bobble.
-  On a 2, the LMG is affected.  The weapon malfs and the attack continues with the Fire Strength reduced by 1/2 the firepower (round up) provided by the LMG at this range for the remaining men.
-  On a 3, the rifle is affected.  However, at RR0 it provides no firepower (but it is STILL considered "firing") so the rifle malfunctions and there is no effect on fire strength on the attack.  At any other range, it is providing FP, the rifle Is malfed and the rest of the attack is resolved reducing the FS by 1/2 FP provided by the rifle (round up).

Now let's say the crewman and the rifleman were pinned (Only the LMG is unpinned.  STILL all three are considered "firing").  If a Red 6 RNC is drawn, all three could be affected, but if the RPC(3) chooses a pinned man (either the crewman or rifleman) then the weapon simply breaks with no effect on FS for the rest of the attack, because a pinned man was chosen.  If the LMG were selected, the normal penalties apply.

However, if a Red 5 RNC were drawn, the only weapon that could be affected is the now uncrewed LMG ( see 11.1).  (Uncrewed LMGs malf on x5-6.  The MP and rifle malf on x6.) In this case, no RPC is required and the LMG automatically breaks with the normal penalties.

Yes, it confusing.  Stick to the errata on all malfunction rules.

When you set up Scenario A

AX RC   0   1   2   3   4   5
--------- G

AL RC    5   4   3   2   1   0
---------------------- G

The opposing groups are both at Range Chit 0.   The "distance" between them is 5, and to calculate relative range it's 5-5 = 0.

--------- G

query: Range.: It seems to me that it would make sence to add your range to a FP resolution...but this isn't so, right?
title: Range.
raw_question: It seems to me that it would make sence to add your range to a FP resolution...but this isn't so, right?
ground_truth_answer:
No, range is not used in this manner.  

In a firepower attack (rifles, MGs, BARs, flamethrowers), range is used to determine how much firepower each man has available (closer = more) vs opposing groups.  The total amount of firepower of all men in a group determines how large of fire cards you can play.  The total firepower must be >= the circled number on the Fire card (or, if using more than one fire card, the total FP must be >= the total of the circled numbers on the fire cards and starting Fire Strength will total FS on all of the Fire cards.).

More firepower you have in a group means:
-  More Fire cards will become usable.
-  Those now usable Fire cards will also have higher Fire Strengths.
-  You will be more likely to be able to use multiple Fire cards in an attack.

In an Ordnance attack (mortars, AFV main guns, Infantry guns, AT weapons), range determines the To Hit numbers (generally, closer=more likely to hit, except mortars can get too close).   Also more likely to get a hit, the greater chance of getting a particularly effective hit.

Yes and yes.  And you take moving fire penalties.....

The key to flanking is the playing of a Flank movement card places a Flank Fire chit on adjacent enemy group (subject to that group having a front group.)  The Flank Fire chit doubles the FP, but any affects of moving fire remain in effect (1/2 FS, 1/2 FP Bolt action rifles, unbracketed crewed FP).

But you only lose the Flank Fire chit:
- The Flanked opposing group plays Movement (even to remove wire/unsuccessful fords) or terrain.
-  Your Flanking group plays Movement, has Wire played on it or rejects terrain.
-  Your front group is eliminated or moves away.

Note: playing (or accepting opposing terrain) removes the Movement card, but retains the Flank Fire chit.  So you should get into terrain ASAP so you can that sweet doubled FP.

Shoot!  (see what I did there!)

First question: when firing at the enemy I draw 2 red 6. Is it correct that my second RPC is done on the whole group even though I already have a malfunction cheat in place and in case the RPC points to the same personality card as the the previous, it has no effect because I would have 2 malfunctions on the same personality card?

Not quite.  When resolving a fire attack (not an ordnance attack or demo charge attack, which has different rules) and you draw a malfunction number, you temporarily halt resolving the attack.  then you determine which man the had malfunction occurred  (in some cases this is automatic:  a sole weapon firing (also remember weapons with 0FP at the current range are considered FIRING) or that can break on Red 5 and a Red 5 (not Red 6) was drawn--Japanese/Italian LMG's and uncrewed MG's,  firing flamethrower or captured enemy weapon) which usually requires drawing an RPC to determine the man affected (Note this RPC include ALL men in the group (except transferring men) even those who are not firing:  crewman of MG's, unarmed men,pinned men, men with malfed weapons, etc.)

Once you determine the man who had the malfunction, then you determine the penalty:
-  Firing Crewman:  no malf, but subtract 1 from the remaining attack for "bobbling" the belt.
-  Non firing ordnance/flamethrower or crewman or unarmed man:  N/E.
-  Pinned or men with malfed weapon: No effect on FP, but malf (remove on second malf) the weapon
-  Otherwise, weapon breaks immediately and reduce Fire Strength by 1/2 the firepower of the now broken weapon, rounded up.  (Remove an a captured enemy weapon)

If you find this difficult to remember, use my flow charts which can be downloaded from the file section.

Only now do you continue the attack (unless a sole weapon broke) and if second malfunction number occurs (remember malfed weapons always only break on X6, even if they normally would break on X5-6), it just occurs exactly the same way as before, except you may have an additional malfed weapon.....  

Second question: is it correct that I can repair only one weapon per turn? so if in one turn I collected 2 malfunctions I can repair only one per turn. It is strange. that's how I read the rules, even if it seems strange to me that only one tries to fix his weapon, what does the other do in the meanwhile? looks around? smokes a cigarette? curses his weapon?

-  Mortar guy (with the crewman's help) fires a shell, what are the other guys doing?  Nothing!
-  A few men try infiltration or enter close combat or try to individually transfer.  What are the other guys doing?  Nothing!
-  Attempt to pick up a dropped weapon.  What are the other guys doing?  Nothing.
-  Changing position of a man in the group and/or assigning a new crewman.  What are the other guys doing?  Nothing!

Because armored vehicles often did move through an enemy infantry group.  Now I have played 1000s of game and overrun has come maybe a half dozen times.  I usually use my tank's long range weaponry and never get to overrun range.  (Exception: One scenario "Wasp on Hornet's Nest" which features a Wasp (basically a Bren carrier equipped with a flame thrower--flame on!)

1. Presumably the enemy Group can no longer move backwards. If I conduct another Overrun I can move back through them. If I perform a Lateral Group Transfer I can move to an adjacent 'identity'.

Because after advancing after the groups will be "RR6", the enemy group could  retreat to RR5, but no further.  And once the AFV gets back RR5, they could overrun and then retreat to get back to RR4.  Yes, the AFV can laterally transfer to--subject to normal rules.  One thing you did not ask is could this create an Encircle situation against the overran group: no per the errata.

2. It seems I still defend with my normal armor value despite them being behind me and possibly an AT weapon in front of me (in another identity).

If the group has an AT weapon, then ARMOR/FLANK would be used if attacked with at weapon.  And since an overrunning AFV would sideways Movement card on it, it would use FLANK defense values. 

Which means don't do an overrun vs. a group with AT weapon in the hands of an unpinned man--unless you are desperate.
 
3. I'm not Encircling or Flanking the enemy Group and a friendly Group cannot use me as part of an Encirclement.
Correct vs.. the group being overrun, though the AFV could be Flanking or encircling an ***adjacent group*** if the other requirements are met.  (Front group, Flank movement card, RR6 to adjacent group, etc.)  See 29.2.

4. There doesn't seem to be any rule preventing any Group from moving beyond an adjacent enemy Group and then using Lateral Group Transfer to assume the same identity as the enemy Group but 'behind them'. 

Correct.  It just rarely happens in actual play.

 5. The errata for 29.5 seems to use the wrong reference (should be 17.6) and misunderstand the question, which is can the AFV play a card to Encircle an adjacent Group?

No,  the question asks if after advancing post overrun can AFV form an encirclement against the opposite not adjacent group.  The reference to 20.5 is incorrect.

In practice, these things come up very rarely, if at all, in actual play.

raw_question:
Gents,

I understand the RR ideas of adding each side's RR chits and if over 5 then subtract form 10 to get current RR and so on...all good.

However, when and how are the (-) negative number chits used? I don't understand how they are applied in the game. I can see how the math of +3 + -2 = 1, etc works but when are these chits actually allowed to be placed as per 5.51 RETROGRADE?

"A group may not retreat if, in so doing, it will decrease the Relative Range between it and the closest enemy group to < 0. However, even if an enemy group is close enough to allow a Retreat, a group already at range chit 0 (or less) may play a Movement card in the Retreat mode only if that Movement card is also a red RNC. 

What does the above bold text indicate or is saying?

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you
ground_truth_answer:
Retrograde movement occurs when a group retreats from Range Chit 0 (RC0.)  or a negative range chit. This usually happens in rear guard action / fighting retreat scenarios.  (I.e. D, P, Q, V)

Retrograde movement is simply playing a movement card in retreat mode when the retreating group is at RC0 or a negative range chit.  It has a couple additional requirements:
-  the closest opponent's group must be closer than RR0--applying all normal RR rules including sideways adjastment from A to C. (Attacker Groups are  at 1, 1, 2, the defender groups are at -1 -1.  Defender group B is at RR1 (2 +( -1) = 1) to Attacker Group C can legally retrograde move.  But defending group A iis at RR0 to all opposing groups (1 + (-1) =0 or 2 + ( - 1) -1 =0)  so cannot.

Basically you cannot run away to RR-1 or further to all opposing groups.

-  The movement card card used to retreat must have a Red RNC printed on it.  (Sideways or forward movement can still use either a black or red movement card.)

It make rear guard action / fighting rtreat scenarios interesting.  The defender is being chased, but will slowed down bhy having fewer effective movement cards.

title: Can a group with pinned men reject terrain?
raw_question:

ground_truth_answer: As long as the terrain is a type that's placement is normally allowed to be rejected, the moving group with pinned men can still reject it. query:
Infantry Gun DYO points: DYO question: I am trying to create some Chinese Nationalist Troop Personalities  in the original 1983 format. Based on the history I read  I designed the Infantry Guns based on Chinese versions of German 37mm PAK36 (German Personality card #28)  and the Chinese version of the Italian 47mm ATG M35 (Italian Personality card #30).   I took the stats (based on what I read) and DYO points from the German card and the Italian card but noticed the less effective 37 mm ATG at effect 1 was worth 213 points and the 47 mm ATG at effect 2 was worth 142 points. 

Is there any historical precedence and/or availability issue on why the weaker ATG is worth more points?
title: Infantry Gun DYO points
raw_question:
DYO question: I am trying to create some Chinese Nationalist Troop Personalities  in the original 1983 format. Based on the history I read  I designed the Infantry Guns based on Chinese versions of German 37mm PAK36 (German Personality card #28)  and the Chinese version of the Italian 47mm ATG M35 (Italian Personality card #30).   I took the stats (based on what I read) and DYO points from the German card and the Italian card but noticed the less effective 37 mm ATG at effect 1 was worth 213 points and the 47 mm ATG at effect 2 was worth 142 points. 

Is there any historical precedence and/or availability issue on why the weaker ATG is worth more points?
ground_truth_answer:
Just from running numbers and playing with the values, I can say for sure that there is an underlying formula that was used to produce the DYO point values for guns and tanks (I don't know exactly what it is, but it clearly exists). But they're wildly inaccurate in terms of actually representing the value of the cards in play. In practice most of the vehicles and IGs in the game are unusable in DYO because the points don't reflect their actual value (they overate armor and boxed firepower, which are rarely relevant in play in practice, as well as secondary weapons).

Infantry Guns are once of the dicier elements of the game. IGs as antitank weapons represent poor play value; tank duels are just not very compelling in Up Front. They are only used in scenario H, not one of the better scenarios in the game. The DYO values for these weapons are particularly useless in practice.

In practice, here is what I bet happened: the Up Front team came up with a formula for valuing guns and tanks which everyone knew was not particularly precise. Then they just playtested scenario F (or whatever) until they got it close, and they reverse-engineered the DYO template value for the scenario from their inaccurate AFV valuations. Scenario F's victory conditions are very close to A; the defender "wins ties", but that's not such a large advantage that you would think the attacker needs a huge 471:279 point force advantage in F compared to 241:241 for A. The DYO value of the attacker's force is wildly inflated because the tank is overpriced. This is why in free-form DYO scenarios like the 501 City Fight in 4 you only ever see a tiny number of vehicles, the ones where the point value formula AH came up with back in the day happened to produce a value that was actually kind of close (so, not heavily armored, no boxed firepower, no secondary weapon).

So here is my takeaway from all of these observations. If you want to expand the game to new IGs and new tanks, the best ones to do are actually not the AT guns that Avalon Hill focused on - I'd start with infantry guns or heavy mortars. The NRA had a variety of older infantry guns and smaller artillery pieces, as well as heavier mortars, that might fit the bill and be generally useful in Up Front. You can extrapolate the formulas for infantry PCs (look at the mortars) to come up with a pretty fair value for these. For tanks, the only thing that makes sense in the game is light armor that could be used in F, so I'd focus on the various armored trucks and Soviet and German-built armored cars and light tanks they had available. Some of these are the same vehicle as is in another nationality's inventory. If you're designing your NRA special rules suite to put them on par roughly with the Soviets in terms of hand rules and special capabilities, just copy & paste the stats and then mark the point value of a British or German vehicle down by 20%. If you want to ding their crew morale down to 4 from 5 add about another 15-20% to the discount. The point values for light tanks that are armed mostly with an MG or small gun and have light armor are the closest to being rational, and if you use them just to re-build scenarios E and F, it'll work out OK. Then if you want to include (say) lend-lease Shermans for X and Y Force, you'll just need to put them into a variation of scenario G or H and then playtest it until the balance is right. Another note: if you're designing them as a comparable to the Italians, the AH formula for infantry is broken for the Italians. The Italians are priced the same as the Soviets, but in practice are much worse. So you'd have to create another "tier" below the Soviets with a point value multiplier of .7 or something to make the DYO values fair, but this is just a design cul-de-sac. Make sure they're no worse than the Soviets.

AH uses "Flank" in two different ways:  Flanking Fire and Flank boxed defense values.  (They really should have called the latter "Side defense values" or something similar.)

Basically the AFV uses Flank defense values when:
-  The AFV is moving in sideways mode.
-  AFV being flanked by the enemy.

have you ever offered an opponent a "good" terrain,  Offering brush as RR 3 or higher makes sense.  

I know what you are thinking--he wouldn't have moved without having a Woods or Bldg and si putting in less valuable terrain (or force him to give up advancement).  

But your opponent can follow the same logic: if you had a Stream. Wire or usable good Fire card, you would have used it!  Your opponent might have a couple options if he accepts the Brush:
-  If he has good Fire card, he'll get the first shot.  That may have been his reason he was advancing to RR3 in first place.  By offering terrain, it allowed your opponent to start firing a turn sooner.
-  if he has another Movement card (and he well might to ptotect against a Stream or Wire), and then he'll Move to his better terrain anyway, and maybe advance again.  Unless you drew something painful on this turn, probably still don't have one.

I did this a few times early in my Up Front "career", either of the above was often my more experienced opponent's response.

I suppose if you have the mortar you'd consider offering them a woods card.  

This has more merit.  Your opponent will likely accept as it is good terrain--except, of corse, against mortars/artillery.  Mortars are excellent weapons--getting Effect # + RNC up to 3 (4 with acquisition) can be very deadly.  And you can use any fire card.    But you will miss from time to time (and Murphy's Law dictates the mortar will break on the first shot.  D'oh!  🤢 ), 

The only tactical thing to consider with a building/wall is they can't cycle cards by attempting to entrench but I don't think that's a good trade-off.    

Agreed not a good trade off.

A more important reason to offer good terrain is for scenario VCs, particularly B City Fight, N Jungle Mtg.  Especially late in the final deck, offer anything other Bldg/Jungle.

Group A has Movement+movement+smoke on top, now defending. 
What are the modifier applied to the attack to that group? All three? (+1 +1 -1)
And if it was
Movement+smoke+movement+smoke?

Thanks

title: Movement+smoke
raw_question:
Hi
Group A has Movement+movement+smoke on top, now defending. 
What are the modifier applied to the attack to that group? All three? (+1 +1 -1)
And if it was
Movement+smoke+movement+smoke?
Well, I know the answer for m+s+m (clearly explained in the rules), actually I don't know how to count a smoke on top of the pile, I don't think it dismisses the first movement modifier, but I wanted to make sure
Thanks
V
ground_truth_answer:
Two key rules here:
7.2. This rule specifies that if the top.card on a group is a movement card, then only  the next movement or terrain card applies.
13.1. Smoke (and wire) modifies the last terrain card played.  (At the beginning of the game, lack of a terrain card = open ground.)

Note:  the rule 13.1 does NOT say Smoke modifies Movement cards, only the last terrain card played.  That would mean if  two movement cards are in play on a group, any Smoke modifies the prior terrain, but that terrain would not count per 7.2.

But examples B & C  under rule 13.25 clearly contradicts this.  (Far from the only place where AH effectively vetoed a rule with an example.)  Given other situations discovered before, I am assuming the example is what AH intended.

So it should be played as any Smoke under 2 or more Movement cards is ignored (per example C as the Smoke modified a terrain card (or virtual Open Ground) which no longer counts.) But any Smoke above the second Movement card (in a stack with 2 or more movement cards) is counted (per example B, but I'm not sure of the terrain being modified....)

That being said, Smoke is rarely played while a group is moving.  It is usually played before you start moving a group, then move the group, then place the group in terrain.  

If you must Move twice (desperate times can require desperate measures), using an extra turn to play the Smoke after the first Movement card provides little extra cover (which might get blown away) at the additional chance for the opponent to fire at the group or put it in Wire or a Stream.

Only once ALL of my groups have withdrawn successfully, the game ends (thus 42.72 "and the scenario ends immediately" is completely misleading and in conflict with 42.73?). 42.72 does not use the words "ends immediately" in its text.  What is variant A and Variant B?  What are you talking about?

3. The opponent can pursue and prevent the withdrawal of a group by keeping/moving one of his groups to RR5 to a withdrawing group AND passing a morale check with his unpinned SL (the SL can be anywhere on the board, he doesn't need to be part of the "pursuing" group). The morale check does not count as an action for the SL's group - it's free. 

4. A group trying to withdraw will keep trying automatically every turn? Thus, the pursuing player needs to keep his group at RR5 and his SL needs to pass a morale check every single turn in order to prolong the game?

VARIANT B) Prolonging the game after victory by squad break or scenario victory conditions

1. Once he has fulfilled the scenario's victory condition or has broken the opponent's squad, the victorious player can try to prolong the game by passing a morale check with his unpinned squad leader. The morale check does not count as an action for the SL's group - it's free. If the check succeeds, another round is played (and the SL may test again for another round, etc). If the check fails, the game ends. 

I will just explain the rule:

Basically a scenario in a Campaign game can end in 4 ways:
-  Voluntary withdrawl and concession  by one side per 42.6.
-  Squad break
-  Victory conditions.
-  End of final deck.

On the winning player's winning turn or turn following his opponent's announcement of a withdrawl of a group, the winning player may declare a pursuit, if there are cards left in the deck-so no pursuits if won by time limit.  His active SL (including ASL promoted to SL due SL elimination per errata) must pass a morale check to initiate pursuit (Failure = no pursuit will be attempted.)  This is done once during the game.  Often a winning player will reject pursuit if the potential additional casualties wouldn't be worth the additional advantages (usually just a few elan points).  If the pursuit was not initiated, either voluntarily or failure of the morale check, the game end immediately at the end of the winning player's turn.

If a group attempts withdrawl, it succeeds on the next turn unless the opponent both initiates pursuit (or had initiated pursuit previously) and has a group @ RR5 to the withdrawing group. Since the withdrawing group is in the act of retrograde movement (i.e. retreating to a negative range chit), the pursuing group must usually move forward to be at RR5.  If at the end of the next turn, if pursuit was not declared or no persuing enemy groups are at RR5, the withdrawing group is removed from play--it succeded in its withdrawal. A group that is encircled cannot attempt withdrawal.

Once a pursuit is declared, the game now ends with if all opposing groups are withdrawn (or eliminated) OR the end of the next deck.  (This is why you can't pursue when win on time limit.)

A) Yes the terminology is confusing, but it helps to call the position of a group as Range Chit #  or RC# and use the term "Relative Range" for the total of range chits with the correction for lateral distance and passing an adjacent group.  (5.6 & 5.61)

B) On the turn ***following*** the turn when the banzaiing group reaches RR5, the banzaiing must enter close combat.  (You can't do it the same turn as that would give the banzaiing group two actions in one turn: moving and entering CC).  Also the banzaiing group must enter CC each turn it remains at RR5.  If the defending group moves away, the Banzaiing group could move this turn to get back to RR5 and then enter Cc on the following turn.

C)  Based on 45.43, I would say you could call off banzai after the opponent advanced to evade your group.  There are other rules that get "turned around" if opposing groups pass each other.

D) Why in the Emperor's name are you Banzaiing?   Assuming you can find a Jungle card (i.e.  Woods or Building if playing with a standard deck--there are 13 such cards in the deck), you'd have 20 VP (for the 4 unpinned guys at RC5) for that alone.  You almost certainly have a huge lead.

What if your opponent has a good fire card? You are moving with at least 1 movement card in play (remember the movement card to call for Banzai remains in play.) If two or more movement cards are in play (which would have happened with the movement you described), your TEM is +2--terrain has no effect.  AND you can't play concealment cards and all pin results against you are KIAs.  I can't think of a faster way to lose 20 VPs and give 10 VP to your opponent.

Even if your opponent can only muster a Fire 1, you might easily lose 2 or 3 guys.  

Almost any other action is preferable:  infiltrate to enter CC the normal way, fire if able, or even rally.

title: Infantry attacks against an AFV
raw_question: Can regular infantry, say a crewed LMG, attack the morale and CE defense values of an AFV with regular FP?
ground_truth_answer:
On rereading, there is two sources of boxed fp:
- Flamethrowers 
- all other personality cards have a boxed fp of 1 vs. OT AFVs at RR5  (In addition, to their normal unboxed fp.)

If the fire card uses fp <= the amount boxed fp available vs. an AFV, then 2 resolutions are performed:
- first vs. Morale and CE values
- next vs. Armor or Flank values.
(See 22.5 & 28.7)

If the fp of Fire card > the boxed fp available (but <= unboxed fp), then only the unboxed vs. Morale/CE occurs.

Note:  This particular rule is very rarely used. I don't know if I have ever used it--mostly due to few AFV vs. FT scenarios.

query: Order of resolution of multiple CC: If I attack a group in CC, and there are multiple CCs to resolve, can I choose which CC to resolve first? I can't find anything in the rules which rules on this one way or another.
title: Order of resolution of multiple CC
raw_question: If I attack a group in CC, and there are multiple CCs to resolve, can I choose which CC to resolve first? I can't find anything in the rules which rules on this one way or another.
ground_truth_answer:
There are some issues with the Squad Break rule.

 First, the squad break rule, in full, reads:  16.5 BROKEN SQUAD:  A scenario always ENDS (emphasis added) whenever a player has lost more than half of his personality cards due to KIA and/or rout.  Reinforcements are not considered part of the force until they actually enter play. 

Note: later expansion rules for Japanese, French and Italians modified the percentage of losses.  Errata also clarified simultaneous loss in the same CC pair and prisoners or surrendered men count.

The rule itself does NOT say the player suffering a squad break loses.  OOPS!  Though the immediately following example does say the player "loses immediately", and everyone I have encountered has interpreted it that way.
I am another who interprets the squad break rule according to the example, which I think is quite clear (IIRC, it's not the only case in which Up Front hides basic rules in examples).

This creates a rather odd paradox: an attacker is not allowed to call off a series of CCs per 20.52 and 20.62, so he cannot say "well I am now down to 1 man from breaking, so I'll stop here without resolving the rest of the CC matchups."  But by squad break  immediately interpretation, the player can stop here when squad break is acheived,  without resolving the rest the CC matchups--even if resolving them may result in both sides ending up broken.

I am not saying "squad break causes immediate loss and thus cancels remaining CCs" is incorrect.  (I would lean towards say it is correct, but I am not 100% sure.)  But it is built on a foundation of mud.
This is an interesting paradox indeed Richard. If an attacker is not normally allowed to call off a series of CCs, and if the rules, in other circumstances, even expressly instruct us to continue the game after its normal conclusion if a CC attack has begun, then it does make sense that a CC would continue after a squad breaks in the event of there being a chance of the other squad breaking too. This interpretation has the merit of being both more dramatic, and of requiring a bit more tactical subtlety on the part of a player seeking to end a close game with CC. That I like, but it's something of an irresistable force in the face of the immovable object that is the "loses immediately" citation from the example immediately following rule 16.5. I think this citation has some bearing on the matter:
16.5 Two players are both in danger of having their squad broken. During a close combat struggle, the random draw results in a tie,
eliminating both combatants, and both squads are broken. Is the game a tie, with both sides losing? If not, how is victory determined?
A. It counts as a loss for both players.
In the end though, it looks to me like this one is an example of 'you pays your money and you takes your choice', to be decided, in the absence of an authorative ruling, by a gentlemen's agreement between opponents.

Dear Sirs,

I recently played the Italians, including personality card #28, PFC Ritondo w/ his Anti-Tank Rifle and I've got a coupla questions:

1. His "To Hit" values include bracketed values, so I assume he needs to be crewed for full use of the Anti-Tank capability, but he also has a firepower value of "1", w/ no corresponding bracketed value--can he thus be used uncrewed and still provide this firepower?

2. Along the same lines, if he is uncrewed, but you are just using it for the firepower, and a red "5" is drawn, does he qualify for potential malfunction?  His malfunction values are "X6, ".

Request references and rationale, plz.

Andrew
ground_truth_answer:
Dear Sirs,

I recently played the Italians, including personality card #28, PFC Ritondo w/ his Anti-Tank Rifle and I've got a coupla questions:

1. His "To Hit" values include bracketed values, so I assume he needs to be crewed for full use of the Anti-Tank capability, but he also has a firepower value of "1", w/ no corresponding bracketed value--can he thus be used uncrewed and still provide this firepower?

No, like all crewed weapons it may be fired when not fully crewed, but at less firepower or worse to hit # and higher malfunction rating.  It does not need to be crewed for AT capability or when used vs. Personnel.

As for use against personnel, it has 1 fp at all ranges regardless of whether if it crewed or not.  Like all ATRs.

2. Along the same lines, if he is uncrewed, but you are just using it for the firepower, and a red "5" is drawn, does he qualify for potential malfunction?  His malfunction values are "X6, ".

Yes.  If the ATR is not fully crewed (i.e.  no crewman or a pinned crewman), it has a malf rating of X5-6, which means if a Red 5 is drawn it will usually mean that weapon will be only eligible to break.  (Unless there are 2 or more X5-6 weapons, then you would draw an RPC to determine which X5-6 weapon malfunctions.) If you drew a Red 6, then the RPC includes all X6 weapons as well.

If it were crewed, then its malf is X6 and therefore it only ***potentially*** breaks on a Red 6.  (Because the RPC would include all firing weapons, crewman, malfed weapon specified in the rules.) That's  the risk of firing when it is not fully crewed.

Yes, in practice that means an X5-6 weapon (like a not fully crewed Italian ATR, Italian LMG) an actually breaks far more often than you might think.

Note all of this also true for Japanese ATR which is also a crewed weapon and breaks on the same numbers.

I am more surprised you didn't ask about the To Hit#'s this weapon, which is wrong on the AH card and chit (in different ways!)  This was corrected on the Wargamr Vault edition.

Request references and rationale, plz.

ALWAYS refer to errata on malfunction questions--the editor basically had to rewrite the entire to fix the many issues with it.

As for realism rationale, that a bug (not a feature) of all the malfunction rules.  (More weapons in firing group = less likely for each individual to break due to RPC draw.  More in the target group = more likely to break as there are more RNC draws.)  But to fix these problems would be far worse than not fixing them.

ground_truth_answer:
Thanks for entering to the discussion Richard

Then you adjust for the not being  firing an opposite of adjacent group, so subtract -1  to RR3  (Being further away laterally means harder to hit.)

To be clear I'm not talking about fire, and reading 5.61 it seems that you apply the -1 of Lateral Distance at all times not only to fire (I've been playing scen D, where you need to be at RR5 to win)

Yes.  Fire is the most common reason, these RR adjustments are used in all situations where RR is used: victory conditions where you have a particular RR (Not range chit), flanking, retrograde movement (i.e. must be RR>0 in order to retreat), night rules (for sighting, starshells and allowable retreats), Surrounded scenario, Etc.

Yes, that does mean in Scenario D (4 men at RR5), my Group A at RC 0 and  your group C at RC5 are at RR4 to each other.  In order to win you would need lateral laterally transfer C to B.

What is the rationale that a single Movement card put the advancing group from RR4 to behind the enemy group? (two ranges is this case)

Let's say Group A are RR5 to opposing Group B.  Basically the groups are  "even" each other.  If Group A retreats, then they clearly would now be RR4.  OK.

Now what happen if Group A advances, now the total of the range chits would be 6.  And the Group A would be behind Group B, but the same distance away from each other as they were at RR4.  (That's what the "if the RC total >5, subtract from 10" rule is doing.)

The gives the correct distance for firing.  Now, natural flanking (17.3) and encirclement (17.6) say you have to be "RR4 but behind the adjacent target group" to gain that advantage.  That's the same as RR6!  In this situation Group A would gain Natural Flanking (if there is also Group B as well) or if they then moved sideways on a later turn, gain Encirclement.

So I have a little bit truble separate all different rules of what weapon can be malfunction in a regular fire attack that draws a red 6 RNC.

In rule 19.11 it talks about weapon that ate not considered to be fire.

But later down in text it talks about weapon that still have 0fp are considered to fire.

So weapon that are not firing is weapons lile bazooka etc?

Becouse it seems a crewmans is still targeted by a malfunction event.
ground_truth_answer:
I'll start by saying "You're  welcome", to the many thanks given above.

Malfunction is one the areas of the ruled where so many ideas were included, that that when any question comes up, you can't really point to any one place in the rules.  One question leads to another...... The original errata keeper, Andy Maly, couldn't either.  Basically, my answer above is the whole errata.

I could see what AH was trying to do with malfunction rules.  They wanted different weapons (particularly uncrewed MGs) to have different rates of failure. They wanted the resolution of the attack to be have a lower effect on the remaining men in target group, but they wanted a single weapon that broke to fall silent.  They wanted FTs & captured weapons  to be very prone to failure.  They wanted the possibility of broken weapons to be permanently broken.  They wanted MG belts to temporarily jam. Then they listed each of these ideas as individual rules instead of coming up with a process to determine which rule applies when (which the errata ends up doing)

Could the malfunction rules have been made simpler?  Sure!  They could have made the malfunction occur after the completion of fire attack resolution.  (But that would remove the tactical play order of men in the group--the ones at the end of line have slightly lower fire attacks than the front of the line.  So you put your SL, low morale guys, MG, at the back.  I must confess I enjoy the tactical touches these rules bring, despite the added rules overhead.)

You could get rid 19.11 which creates a big exception that mostly ends up applying only to AFV MG and FTs--because other MGs and FTs are routinely placed in multi man groups.   If I had my way, this rule should simply be junked: after a malfunction, the resolution would always continue with FS reduction.  (Even worse, it was placed before the more commonly applied rule 19.13, giving the impression to some people that 19.11 should have priority.)

And to add to that, from a realism point of view, there are still major issues:
A) The more men in the firing group, the less chance each weapon will break.  (When there are 3 men in the firing group, when a malfunction occurs, 1/3 chance that weapon A breaks.  5 firing men, 1/5 chance weapon A breaks.)
B)  The more men in target group, the greater the chance a weapon breaks.  (Firing at 3 men, 3 chances that the dreaded Red 6 will come up.  5 men, 5 chances.)

But for fixing those issues, the cure would be far worse than the disease.  DO NOT GO THERE!

45.423 ... A Banzai group (or berserk man - ignore [24.7]) can perform Close Combat even while on a Minefield provided it is at Relative Range 5 to its target. query: AFV MG firing while moving: Being a non-ordnance weapon, does an AFV MG firepower get halved for firing while moving? I'm fairly certain it's a yes.
title: AFV MG firing while moving
raw_question: Being a non-ordnance weapon, does an AFV MG firepower get halved for firing while moving? I'm fairly certain it's a yes.
ground_truth_answer:
Being a non-ordnance weapon, does an AFV MG firepower get halved for firing while moving? I'm fairly certain it's a yes.

No.  The firepower is unchanged. but the Fire Strength is halved rounded down (ie the value of EACH fire card.  So Fire 1 and Fire 3 is reduced to Fire 0 + Fire 1)

Fire Strength is always halved when moving non-ordnance is firing.  EXC: Flamethrowers providing all FP to the attack.

Firepower is only halved for bolt action rifles (Semiautomatic rifles N/A) Also fully crewed LMGs use bracketed FP, not in Marsh or Stream.

ground_truth_answer:
I'm having trouble with the relationship between flanking and encirclement. For one thing, they both sound like the same thing. (Edit: To clarify, natural flanking and encirclement sound like the same thing. Or, at least, they sound like they are both the result of getting directly behind an adjacent group)

It sounds like encirclement can only happen after (and due to) flanking. Is this correct?

Are flanking and encircling like a 1-2 punch? First you flank, then you encircle?

Thanks. Sorry if I'm a little thick here. If anyone cares to expound on the relationship between the two, I'd be grateful.

Yes, they are related:  
- To encircle, yes, the "flanking" must be in a natural flanking position (ie. Atotal of range chits =6.) but flank chit may have been subsequently removed.  (Via play of movement or terrain by the flanked group).  
- Like flanking a front group is required.

Once the proper position is achieved, THEN when the flanking group plays a sideways movement, the the opposing group is encircled.  Essentially natural flanking position is a prerequisite by for encirclement.

Once encircled:
-  All FP at the encircled group is doubled from any group (not just from the flanked group.)
- The encircled group cannot  receive or exit individual transferring men.  Or laterally transfer to change its group ID.
-  Panic -1.

To get out of an encirclement requires either:
- elimination of either group forming the encircle (including if either group moved away via lateral transfer.
- the encircled group infiltrates either encircling group, 
- either encircling group is RR1 or further from the encircled group, or
- if both encircling groups end up in front of the encircled group. ie.  The encircled group retreated to get away in these last two situations.)

(In most cases, the encirclement ends when the encircled group is eliminated. ;)  )

ground_truth_answer:
Hello,
I'm a super newbie and going through the rulebook for the first time. I'm not sure what's the meaning of having opposing groups like AvsA, BvsB, etc. 
At the moment the only rule I found is that if you want to fire at a "non adjacent" group you count 1 less range, so less fire power (Like, A has relative range of 3 on B but relative range of 2 on C and D).

Are there any other situations were opposing groups are important in the gameplay?

Thank you.

Point by point:
-  Directly opposing groups (ie A vs A, B vs B, etc) cannot advance past RR5, which means move through each other.  (With the exception of AFV overruns,)
-  Because of the above, for group to reach the required range chit to win, it may have laterally move to group where there is no directly opposite group in order to advance.
-  Flanking opposing group B requires a directly opposing "front group" and and adjacent group at either A or C to flank.  Encirclement also requires 2 groups in the same arrangement.
-  The effective range is increased  by -1 when firing at groups that are directly opposed or adjacent (ie A vs C or D, etc.)  This can affect firepower or To Hit numbers on the weapons.  Also applies in retrograde movement (where at least opposing group must have RR>0) and night scenarios.
-  Infiltration and close combat can only performed against directly opposing or adjacent groups.
-  Generally groups are limited to A-D, except with reinforcements, team play and special scenario rules in three player scenarios.

H'mm.  The Berserk rule says:

and doesn't mention Concealment, so I'd assume that the normal rules for CC apply, allowing play of Concealment by both sides.

ground_truth_answer:
4.2 ACTION CAPABILITY: A player turn consists of a player performing a maximum of one action in each group of Personality cards he controls.
"Consists of" is a bit unfortunate because, yes, that can imply that a turn is composed entirely of the things listed after that phrase -- in this case, a player taking actions.  
And at 4.3 DISCARD CAPABILITY it seems to imply that your turn is finished, for example:
4.31 A German player may always discard one (but never more than one) unused card from his hand, regardless of the number of actions he performed during his turn.
This doesn't buttress the claim that a turn is composed only of a player taking actions.  The turn could have many phases, including a taking actions phase.  So, "regardless of the number of actions performed during his turn" doesn't limit the turn scope to just the actions part of the turn.

But then, at 4.5 HAND REFILL it says:
[...] bring the total number of cards in his hand up to his full allotment (EXC: 15.2). It is now the opposing player's turn.
For me, this is the most clear statement.  And the most logical.  This states when one player's turn ends and the other's begins.  So I agree with the opinion that the entire turn consists of taking actions plus drawing to refill the hand.
