query:
AFV Bog: Can someone explain the AFV Bog and Un Bogging rule to me please.

JB.
title: AFV Bog
raw_question:
Can someone explain the AFV Bog and Un Bogging rule to me please.

JB.
ground_truth_answer:
AFVs have a BOG rating printed on them (e.g. BOG: 4/w7).  Whenever a Gully, Woods, or Stream terrain card is played (and accepted) on an AFV or whenever a Wire card is played on an AFV, you check to see if it is bogged.

To check, draw a card and consult the appropriate group column at the bottom of that card.  In the example above, if it was Gully, Woods or Stream, you'd check the 4c column.  If it was Wire, you'd check the 7w column.  If the number in the column is red, place a Bog chit on the AFV.  It can no longer move until the chit is removed.

To remove the Bog chit, play a Movement card into the discard pile and draw a card.  If the RNC # (i.e. the number at the top right) is black, remove the chit.

ground_truth_answer:
Excerpt from Bonzai:

48. RANDOM REINFORCEMENTS-

48.1 Random Rei.nforcement is used in conjunction with the rules for Reinforcements (35)and can be used only when cited by SSR or at a cost of 50 points per Deck in a DYO scenario (43). Note that a player could purchase the Random Reinforcement capability for only a fraction of a scenario's length, but in that case would be entit led to attempt to gain Random Reinforcement only during the Deck paid for. Reinforcements would not have to arrive during the Deck paid for.

48.2 A player may attempt to earn Random Reinforcement immedlately only during his next player turn following his opponent's drawing of a black 6 RNC (the card must have been used by him as a RNC; not as a RPC, action, or discard). If the player elects to try for reinforcements, he may do so by drawing a RNC as his sole action for that player turn. If he draws a red RNC he receives no reinforcements, but if he draws a black RNC he has succeeded in gaining reinforcement and immediately checks the Random Reinforcement Table to determine the extent of his reinforcements as per the RNC drawn. The reinforcements received do not appear on the table immediately, but must enter as per 35.3-.4 in a subsequent turn. The player may also attempt Random Reinforcement in his first turn following the shuffle of a deck in which he was eligible for Random Reinforcement. However, in both cases, if a player does not attempt Random Reinforcement in his very next player tum he loses that capability until another opportunity (an opponent's drawing of a black 6 RNC or end of a qualifying deck) presents itself.

48.21 Russian Entrenchment altempts and Japanese Movement, although not counted as actions for Discard purposes, are not allowed during a player turn in which that player attempts to gain Random Reinforcement. A Hero card is the only card which can be played during a player turn in which Random Reinforcement is attempted.

48.22 No discards are allowed during a player turn in which Random
Reinforcement is attempted, except for the Japanese free Cower card
Discard capability.

48.31 CHOICE: A reinforcement emry listed only as "*" entitles the recipient to choose any one Personnel card available other than a MMG, AT Gun, or AFV. If he chooses a man armed with a rifle or MP he may equip that man with a secondary weapon such as a DC, PF, or ATMM. If he chooses a blank Personnel card, be must use Morale/Panic chits to reflect a Morale/Panic rating of 3/4 respectively regardless of nationality. Whatever his choice, the player must make it immediately: he may nor wait until he actually brings the reinforcements into play.

48.32 SUBSTITUTES: Ifa designated reinforcement personnel card is not available because it is already in play or that weapon is not available during the year the scenario is being played, substitution is made according to the following order of priorities:
	A. A personnel card with the same weapon and Morale/ Panic values (use blanks or other personnel cards with the same weapon and appropriate Morale/Panic value chits).
	B. A personnel card with another weapon worth the same or less points as listed on the unavallable reinforcement.

48.33 ENTRY: Random Reinforcement may enter at Group E or Z. Reinforcements which enter with a Movement card which is a red RNC must enter as Group Z. Reinforcements which enter with a Movement card which is a black RNC must enter as Group E. If a Group E or Z is already in place thus blocking entry of reinforcemems along that edge, the reinforcements may not enter along that edge until the blocking group has been moved or eliminated. Reinforcements may not use Individual Transfer to enter play.

48.4 SNIPER: A Sniper Reinforcement can be used to regain a lost Sniper capabilily, or used to gain Sniper capability for a player who did not start the scenario with that capability. If the player still has a Sniper capability when he gains a Sniper reinforcement, he may attack twice for each Sniper card he plays (or three times if be gains sniper reinforcement twice, etc). Multiple sniper attacks using the same Sniper card must draw a separate RPC to determine the recipient of each attack (unless there is only one card in the only attacked group). This dual Sniper auaek capability can also be used in DYO scenarios where additional snipers are purchased.

48.41 The Sniper player has the option to split his multiple Sniper attack between different groups or apply all shots against the same group, but must predesignate the group(s) to be attacked before the first attack is resolved.

48.42 A successful Sniper Check (14.4) eliminates only one sniper, not a player's entire multiple Sniper capability. Each group attacked by a sniper is still allowed the option of only one Sniper Check as its sole action for that turn regardless of the number of times it was attacked by one or more Sniper cards during that turn.

48.43 Sniper reinforcements do not have to be brought into play by a Movement card (35.3) as do other reinforcements. They are automatically available in the next player turn.

query:
Playing a Fire card: Can one play a fire card whilst they have am active movement card.

JB.
title: Playing a Fire card
raw_question:
Can one play a fire card whilst they have am active movement card.

JB.
ground_truth_answer:
Yes. You have some restrictions like having to halve the firepower of bolt-action rifles and using the bracketed LMG value if it is crewed, and remembering not to count the firepower of non-crewed LMGs or any MMGs/HMGs. 

Important note:  "crewed" should be fully crewed for the LMG (ie main weapon bearer and crewman must both be unpinned.)

Then you must halve the Fire Strength of the Fire Card itself. You can fire however.

Halve the Fire strength of each Fire CARD, rounding each down if necessary.  So if firing with a Fire 3 and a Fire 1 while moving totals to 1.  So unless you need to get rid of the Fire 1 card, don't play it on it a moving group.

Or even better, stop moving first, preferably in good terrain, before firing.

AH limited themselves to three lines of help text.  (This was even before Twitter.  :)   or  WYSIWYG publishing software so adding more lines and reformatting the art on those cards would have been a hassle.)

query:
DRAFT Player Aid for Combat Results - Please Review: For some reason I can never remember how Routing works for this game. I do not know why there is a mental block, but it is there. What did I screw up this time?

title: DRAFT Player Aid for Combat Results - Please Review
raw_question:
For some reason I can never remember how Routing works for this game. I do not know why there is a mental block, but it is there. There is chance that I will FINALLY get to teach this game, so I thought I would address this simple block with a simple flow chart!

What did I screw up this time?

Thanks.
ground_truth_answer:
Juno has posted a link to my flow charts which covers this on page 3.

Essentially how I present this is:
- Final result number (FRN) = Final Fire Strength + RNC.

- Does RNC cause a malfunction? If Yes, check for which weapon and effect 

- If FRN > KIA  then KIA
- If FRN = KIA then check wound and it no wound then KIA.
- If pinned and >= Panic then check for rout (and then check for wound, or take prisoner at RR5) / KIA (or berserk if Russian at RR5).
- If not pinned and >= Morale then pin man
- Then No effect

-  If RNC has BREEZE, remove Smoke cards and adjust FRN if needed.

-  Repeat with next man.

The problem with the way you have it is for men whose Panic value is less than their Morale value (i.e. Italians, partisans, etc.) so that per your flow chart, Panic <= FRN < Morale. Per your chart the first thing checked is FRN >= Morale  (No, therefore no effect), but such a man still would panic (because FRN >= Panic value) 

Also Panic makes no difference to an unpinned man and Morale no difference to a pinned one.

Has anyone attempted a complete rewrite of the rules, beginning to end, clarifying all the unclear ideas and including errata and the like?

Not that I need another project, but it is intriguing.
ground_truth_answer:
I guess I just prefer the legalese style. With games like Band of Brothers that use the prose style, I can never find what I'm looking for, it's always buried in a paragraph. I suppose the prose style might be good for first learning, but the case style is much handier for looking things up once you know the game.

This is spot on.  Legalese style is perfect for when rule debate occurs ... as well as minimizing rule debates ... while prose tends to drum up more arguments.  After you learn the rules ... prose doesn't matter anymore ... I just want to cut to chase and find specific rule .. not read about some obscure idea.

No it is "Spot off".  For two very important reasons:
- The rules give no feel to how the game is set up, how it is played, how do you DO these various things like firing,like relative range, like movement, etc.
- Because of the use of Programmed Instruction, items are organized by which scenario that AH decided to introduce the rule, but not any sort of logical.

Because of this Up Front is harder to learn than it should be ***AND*** harder to find the rules you needs a refresher on when you play.  They fail as a teaching aid and fail as reference guide.

An extended illustrated sample game would help the first problem: 
Page 1 here is the set up: German set in two groups A & B, Americans in three groups, A, B & C,  note they set up opposite of reach other.  Each group has an ID chit and range chit value 0.  The deck is located here, the discard here.  Highlight important details like where the SL & ASL are located, that the Germans have a crewed weapon and who is the crew man.  

Page 2: Initial terrain set up.
On the following pages: Include various common actions: Play of a movement card (on a later turn) entering terrain, calculating firepower and conducting a fire attack, rallying men, how to entrench, how to use cars that are played during discards (terrain on opponent, sniper, wire), what happens on a malfunction/repair attempt, etc.

As for the problem of programmed instruction, rules became jumbled all over the place so finding the right is rather difficult.  

Quick, find the rules for entrenchments.  You would THINK this would be early on because this rule isn't complicated and  it's used in EVERY game, but you'd be wrong--AH decided introduce this rule in scenario I.  Same thing with wounds and prisoners in scenario G.  

Why?  Beats me.  These in particular make NO sense.  I can't imagine playing the game at least 10 times before learning how to entrench!

Or rules are scattered about because they apply to multiple items: Terrain and AFV's/mortars/IG's etc. Do you look in the terrain rule section or the weapon rule section?  Or will they be found in both places?  Etc. 

To show how bad this is, look at this example.
The term "hull down" is mentioned EIGHT times before the rules for Hull Down AFV/IG's are explained--most without a rule pointer to reference the rule. 
-  Hills 
-  Wall (No Rule pointer)
-  3 times for it effect on To hit numbers. (1 rule pointer)
-  Mortars (No rule pointer)
-  2 times for TEM and hull down. (1 rule pointer to a subsidiary rule)

When I answer questions on UF rules, I often have to "stitch together"  this rule here and that rule there to get to the correct interpretation which shows how bad the rules are as a reference.

I can think of two major examples as counter points:
-  ASL:  when ASL was created, AH dispensed with programmed instruction, mainly because of the mess SL rules became after the original programmed instruction rule book and changes/contradictions introduced in the first three expansions.  They went with a complete reference format.
-  Combat Commander:  Has a rules reference in outline format, logically laid out and an extended sample of play showing how the game is actually played.  The items in the rule book are sorted in a logical order: Components, Core rules (Sequence of Play, Timing, VC's, Stacking, weapons, ets.)  Each of the Orders (on cards), each of the Actions (on cards), eahc of the events (on cards), Terrain, Fortifications.  Finding what you need to much easier than in Up Front.

Imagine what Up Front's rule book would be like if they were in that format.

The lower net value.  E.g. if the sniper resolution numbers were a Red 3 and a Black 1, the Sniper Check would be against the value of 1.

If random reinforcement grants a sniper and you already have one, you get TWO resolutions per Sniper card played. So having two numbers to check on a sniper check can occur frequently in scenarios with random reinforcements.

Perhaps I'm just missing something, but after reading the malfunction rules several times, something doesn't seem right with the Malfunction Flow chart from the files section.

Following the flow chart, it says: Firing Weapon OR 0FP at Range = Malf Weapon, -1/2 FP to FFS (Round Up).

The problem with this is that the rules plainly state: 

19.13 If the firing group contains more than one weapon with usable
firepower factors, a RPC is immediately drawn to determine which
weapon in the group actually malfunctions. All weapons in an attacking
group (even those with a firepower of 0) are considered to be firing when
the group attacks (EXC: flamethrowers, secondary weapons, ordnance,
non-firing infiltrators, and the weapons of designated crewmen). If the
RPC indicates a non-firing weapon has malfunctioned, there is no effect.
If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a pinned man, there is no
effect to the attack, but the pinned man's weapon does malfunction. If the
RPC indicates a position occupied by a designated assistant crewman of
a firing MG or a man whose weapon has no firepower at its current range,
the malfunction is considered only momentary, and the fire against any
remaining defenders in the defending group yet to be attacked is
resolved with one less Fire Strength, but no weapon malfunctions. If the
RPC indicates a position occupied by a firing weapon, that weapon
malfunctions and combat vs any remaining defenders not yet fired upon
is resolved with one less Fire Strength for every two Firepower factors
(or fraction thereof) previously contributed by the malfunctioned weapon.
This reduction to the Fire Strength is made after any halving effects for
Moving or Night Fire, and is made even if the firing group did not require
that weapon's firepower in order to play the Fire card(s) used in the
attack.

There is another Diamond shaped box that has the result: Assistant Crewman of LMG/MMG = No Malf, -1 to FFS.

According to the rules, it looks like a PC with a "usable" gun whose FP is 0 at its current RR, would only cause any remaining attacks to be resolved with one less FFS not a malfunction to the PC's weapon and -1/2 FP to FFS, as per the result in the diamond shaped box.  I'm wondering if the condition was incorrectly put in the "square box" instead of the "diamond box", thus meaning there's a mistake.
ground_truth_answer:
Please read the errata:

19 Weapon Malfunction
If an Ordnance weapon is firing using the To Hit process (25.3), and the To Hit RNC is in the range of the malfunction values for that weapon, the Ordnance weapon malfunctions, automatically.

If a group is conducting a Fire Attack (6) then ALL weapons in the group are considered to be firing with the following exceptions:
-  Flamethrowers designated as not firing
-  Secondary weapons (e.g. Demo Charge, panzerfaust)
-  Ordnance
-  Non-firing infiltrators
-  Weapons of designated assistant crewmen (however, continue reading) 

If an RNC drawn to resolve the Fire Attack is equal to the malfunction value of only one weapon, that weapon malfunctions automatically, and no RPC is drawn to determine which weapon malfunctions.
Example: Japanese Group comprised of R, R, R, LMG. The RNC is a RED 5. The LMG automatically malfunctions, because it is the only weapon with a malfunction value of a RED 5.

If the group is comprised of only one armed man, that weapon automatically malfunctions, and no RPC is drawn.
Example: In the following four groups: (R; MP; LMG; R, Unarmed Man), no RPC is drawn to determine which weapon malfunctions.

If none of the previous cases applies, then an RPC is drawn to determine which position is affected by the malfunction. Do include Unarmed men, and DO NOT include Men transferring. The following results and their impacts are (use the first case that applies):
-  Unarmed man - no effect.
-  Man is currently pinned - weapon malfunctions, no effect on FS.
-  Ordnance weapon or its designated crewman - no effect. Note that an ATR using FP is not considered firing as ordnance, and therefore both the ATR and the crewman are subject to malfunction.
-  Designated non-firing Flamethrower or Infiltrator - no effect
-  Designated crewman of a firing MG - no malfunction, continue attack with -1 FS
-  Weapon with 0 Firepower at the current range - weapon malfunctions, continue attack with -0 FS
-  Firing weapon malfunctions, and attack continues with one less FS for every 2 FP factors the weapon was contributing to the attack, fractions rounded up. 
Malfunctioned weapons have a base malfunction number of red 6 regardless of the malfunction number printed on the card.

The problem is the original rules contain an oversight which creates a contradiction:
-  Weapons with 0FP at current range are considered to be firing.  The very next line in the long passage you quoted includes:  "If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a firing weapon, that weapon malfunctions and combat vs any remaining defenders not yet fired upon is resolved with one less Fire Strength for every two Firepower factors (or fraction thereof) previously contributed by the malfunctioned weapon."  Which means "firing" 0FP weapon which malfunction break and the Fire Strength of the attack is reduced by 1/2 of firepower of 0 (which equals 0.)

That means there are two rules that tell you what to do with 0FP weapons when they malfunction:
-  0FP weapons don't break and FS is reduced by 1 (per your highlighted rule)
OR 
-  0FP weapons do break and FS is not reduced  (because they are firing).  

The errata keeper (Andy Maly) published this clarification that the latter should apply--Since 0FP are considered "firing", the same penalty as other firing weapons applies when they malfunction.  

It also removes a weird situation where a pinned man with a 0FP weapon (who is clearly NOT firing) has his weapon break, but an unpinned man with 0FP (who IS actually firing) does NOT have his weapon break.  But the same weapon would break at a closer range when the weapon has 1 or more FP.

Basically, Andy had to rewrite the entire malfunction rule because of this and other ambiguities (Weapons that break on different malfunction ranges, ordnance and non-firing weapons in the same group, transferring men, etc.)  Not an easy task!

Any questions on malfunctions should be referred to the errata over the original rulebook.

ground_truth_answer:
I finally got a copy of this game and am very excited to give it a try.  I am currently slogging through the rulebook, which has been tough but encouraging - it seems like a great system.

One thing confusing me is the flanking rules.  I know the rule on natural flanking has been clarified a bit in the errata and over on CSW (you can move sideways into a natural flank - you don't actually have to move from RR5 in the column adjacent to the enemy to RR4 behind the enemy in the column adjacent, as long as you end up in RR4 behind the enemy in the adjacent column one way or another).  While that did clear up some confusion, my remaining question is this:

First off, call "RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy" as "relative range 6".  for most situation that will be the case.  Much easier to understand.

The word forward is emphasized in Rule 17.3--coming in from any direction other than RR5 is not necessarily justifiable, but I think it is common  (Bruce Wigdor's Internet Up Front program apply the "Flanking is at RR6 from any way" interpretation.).  

But moving to natural flank from any position other than RR5 is EXTREMELY RARE.  I don't know if I have seen it 1000's of games.  Just achieving natural flanking is pretty rare.  It just doesn't come up, the attacking player is not going continue pressing forward after passing an adjacent group and/or isn't go way around in order get a natural flank.

Can one unit only naturally flank another unit from RR4 behind? In other words, if I am in RR4 adjacent and behind an enemy, if they move one range unit away from me, or if I move one range unit further away from them, such that we are now at RR3, do I lose my natural flank?

First, you lose the natural flank (or indeed ANY flank), when either the FLANKED group or FLANKING group has a movement card played on it (even to remove wire), the situation you describe cannot happen.  The Flank Fire chit would already be removed.

Second:  No, you cannot initiate natural flanking from RR7. 

A strict reading of the rules would suggest so, but common sense tells me I should still be flanking that unit - just with a little less firepower. 

No, because you lost flank status when either FLANKED group moved or FLANKING group moved. 

My thinking is that I do lose the flank, but I can regain it by lateral flanking? 

Yes, Lateral Flank using a FLANK movement card can be done from ANY relative range.  (Note, relative range is not mentioned in 17.1 & 17.2)

To do this I would have to have a flank movement card and play it sideways - is this correct?  

Yes, as usual for Lateral Flanking.

Or of course I could move back to RR4 and regain the natural flank.

Yes, but I don't think that will happen.  

Basically to initate flanking you need:
-  a FRONT group (i.e. same letter) as the potential FLANKED opposing group.
And either:
-  An adjacent FLANKING group having a FLANK movement card played on it in sideways mode.  (Lateral Flanking per 17.1)
-  An adjacent FLANKING group reaching RR6  (Natural Flanking per 17.3)

Hope this helps.  Flanking is one of the more confusing rules in the game.

query:
Scenario K VCs: I suppose squad break is in effect. Does it have to be achieved twice by Elite force to win (once per scenario segment)?

title: Scenario K VCs
raw_question:
I suppose squad break is in effect. Does it have to be achieved twice by Elite force to win (once per scenario segment)?

Thanks in advance.
ground_truth_answer:
I suppose squad break is in effect. Does it have to be achieved twice by Elite force to win (once per scenario segment)?

Yes, squad break is in effect.  

Winning a scenario segment can be achieved by victory conditions (4 men in one more non-infiltrated groups.....) or breaking the opposing squad.

Once the attacker (i.e. elite squad) completes either VC's or squad break, the game is reset as described in the scenario rules (Attacker forfeiting all men that were KIA'd, Defender receiving all men back. etc.) and the game continues.  The attacker has to complete VC's or opposing squad break a second time to win the scenario.

The defender (i.e. 2nd line squad) need achieve VC's or opposing squad break once to earn the victory.

However, (per published errata) Victory Points are not counted at the end of the final deck.  So, the Defender/2nd line squad will win by avoiding attacker victory conditions.

The rule that specified this was in the errata originally fromthe General:

17.8 When an individual transfer takes place, the group receiving the transfer can not be rearranged at that time (3.3). Where then do the transferring men go? Are the placed at the front of the group, at the back, or can they be placed anywhere they want, just so long as the rest of the group order is not changed?

query: Just getting back into war games after a hiatus and I have a rules question...: When resolving a Sniper attack it looks to me that the RPC draw is made only after the RNC draw to determine if the attack was successful, if the Sniper misses then no RPC is drawn, correct?
title: Just getting back into war games after a hiatus and I have a rules question...
raw_question: When resolving a Sniper attack it looks to me that the RPC draw is made only after the RNC draw to determine if the attack was successful, if the Sniper misses then no RPC is drawn, correct?
ground_truth_answer:
When resolving a Sniper attack it looks to me that the RPC draw is made only after the RNC draw to determine if the attack was successful, if the Sniper misses then no RPC is drawn, correct?

No.  Unless the target group is a single-card group, you first draw an RPC to see which card is the target.  Then you draw an RNC to determine the effect.

14.2     
Playing a Sniper card allows the player to attack one opposing card in a group of his choice regardless of the terrain occupied by that group. If the target group is a multi-Personnel card group, the card to be attacked in that group is determined by a RPC draw (see [14.6]). A Sniper may attack an AFV [28.431] only if its CE value side is face up.

14.3 RESOLUTION:     
A Sniper attack is resolved by drawing a RNC and comparing the number to the KIA & PIN values printed on the Sniper card. There is no significance to the color of the RNC drawn, nor are there any modifications. A "KIA" result removes the defender's Personality card from the game. A "Pinned" result flips his card to the Pinned side. If the defender is already pinned, the Personality Panics and must check for Rout [6.531]. Any other result is a Miss and has no effect. The Sniper card is placed in the Discard pile after resolution. 

This may be important if the player is trying to run the deck down.

Got from the modified rulebook which you can download here in BGG...from the Banzai rules section:

44.9 LMG: The Bren Gun is not considered a crew-served weapon; thus the absence of bracketed
firepower and malfunction values. A Hero card can be used to double the unbracketed firepower values
[10.45] of this weapon only if the Hero card is also a black RNC. This rule cannot be used for other
nationalities (EXC: Japanese).
..................................................................................................................................................................................
44.9 This rule states that the British and (via exception) Japanese non-crew served LMGs can only double its
firepower with the black RNC Hero card, thus implying that the American BAR can use either Hero card.
Specifically "This rule cannot be used for other nationalities (EXC:Japanese)." However, rule 50.6 (DESERT
WAR) states "Like all LMGs in the game which are not considered a crew-served weapon, a Hero card can be
used to double the LMG's firepower only if the Hero card is also a black RNC." Which rule is correct (as they
contradict each other), and how is the BAR handled?
A. Both are; nor do they contradict. The BAR is not considered to be an LMG. Either hero card may be used to
double its firepower.
CLARIFICATION:
The American BAR may use both Hero cards, and is not considered an LMG.
The British LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The French LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The German LMG may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.
The Italian LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The Japanese LMG may only use the Black Hero card.
The Russian LMG may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.

A)  It is not illegal to fire from Group A to Group B, C or D  (though the latter two situations increase the relative range  (see Rule 5.61) meaning you'll have less firepower or more difficult To Hit chance.

B)  Mortars (like all ordnance weapons except the ATR) gain no advantage of flanking position.

C)  All ordnance weapons can be fired with any Fire card.  Ordnance weapons do not have a FIREPOWER value and the number in the circle means nothing.  This makes them very handy--they can use "unusable" high valued Fire cards that clog your hand.

D)  If a group has both regular firepower and mortar, they cannot be used in the same Fire attack or can be combined in in any way to make a larger attack.  Splitting the mortar into a separate group allows attacks with the fire group and mortar on the same turn.

ground_truth_answer:
I see I was being paged here  ;)

LMG/MMG's and Hero cards are kind of kluge of different rules, that can get confusing:
-  Crewable LMG's (G, R) and MMG's double the bracketed firepower per 10.45.  (Even the weapon is not fully crewed (pinned or no crewman--note most players in this situation use the Hero to rally the crewman in this case, so weapon far less likely to malfunction--usually the same amount of FP, but unbracketed malf numbers.)
-  Noncrewable LMG's (B, J, F, I) double their firepower only with Hero card with a BLACK RNC printed on it  (i.e. Card #30, YES; Card #151, NO) per 44.9 & 50.6.
-  BAR's (A) are not considered LMG's, so they double firepower on either Hero card.
-  AFV's:  Rule 28.421 states Hero card cannot be use to improve To Hit numbers or Firepower of AFV's.

The errata confirms that interpretation:

44.9 This rule states that the British and (via exception) Japanese non-crew served LMGs can only double its firepower with the black RNC Hero card, thus implying that the American BAR can use either Hero card. Specifically "This rule cannot be used for other nationalities (EXC: Japanese)." However, rule 50.6 (DESERT WAR) states "Like all LMGs in the game which are not considered a crew-served weapon, a Hero card can be used to double the LMG's firepower only if the Hero card is also a black RNC." Which rule is correct (as they contradict each other), and how is the BAR handled? 
A. Both are; nor do they contradict. The BAR is not considered to be an LMG. Either hero card may be used to double its firepower. 
CLARIFICATION:
The American BAR may use both Hero cards, and is not considered an LMG.
The British, French, Italian & Japanese LMG ‘s may only use the Black Hero card.
The German & Russian LMG’s may use both Hero cards, but doubles its bracketed value.

A realism argument can be made that if a Hero card played to double firepower of a man, the man is maneuvering within his general area (Remember:  The size of UF space is roughly the size of a football field) to get a better shot.  A weapon team wouldn't be mobile enough to take advantage such an advantage.  A weapon wielded by a single man could.

The real reason is more likely that AH thought doubling the unbracketed firepower of a machine gun was just too powerful when they were designing  Up Front.  When Banzai came out, they now had noncrewable LMG's so the Black Hero rule was put in as a compromise.

Also a weapon eligible for tripled FP:  Flank/Encircle/infiltration + Hero, triple whatever firepower it was eligible to double  (i.e. bracketed if it were a crewable LMG)  (Both Heros cannot be played on a single man to triple FP.

title: TO HIT FREQUENCY? God DAMN it!!!!
raw_question:
Can someone please explain what the frick this means? It pisses me off that there is NO reference to FREQUENCY untill this very part and then states it as if I should know what the hell it means...

"25.6 TO HIT FREQUENCY: A To Hit frequency of "0-1" is reduced by one by treating it as a "0", a To Hit frequency of "0" is reduced by one by treating it as a "1", a To Hit frequency of "1" is reduced by one by treating it as a "2", etc. Similarly, a To Hit frequency of "3" is increased by one by treating it as a "2", a To Hit frequency of "1" is increased by one by treating it as a "0", and a To Hit frequency of "0" is increased by one by treating it as a "0-1", etc." 

How the hell can you reduce a number by going UP? I'm getting so sick of these rules! :cry:
ground_truth_answer:
Here's what a frequency chart would look like from highest to lowest:

0-6  162
0-5  156
0-4  146
0-3  130
0-2  108
0-1   80
0     44
1     36
2     28
3     22
4     16
5     10 
6      6

So if the original to hit frequency is, for example, 0-2, and you need to add one to the frequency, it would now hit on 0-3. If the original to hit was only on 0 and you need to subtract one from the to hit, it now hits only on a 1. 

The way this works is there are more zeros than ones in the deck, more ones than twos, more twos than threes, etc.

Grant is absolutely correct--I added the number of cards in the deck for each range to above.

Any +1 To Hit (Acquisition) goes up the list, any -1 To Hit (Concealment, Smoke, Wire, etc.) goes down the list.

It should be noted:
-  If the ordnance weapon malfunctions, the weapon breaks and does not hit.  For example a weapon that breaks on x4-6 on a 0-4 To hit range, breaks on a Red 4. 
-  Normally color of RNC doesn't matter, but...  
If either firer is moving or target is moving (or Hull Down), Red To Hit RNC's are treated as a Miss.  If BOTH are moving, Red To Hit RNC's are treated as a Miss and the To Hit is reduced by -1.

- 25.4 & 25.43 often cause trip ups:  The number (either color) drawn on a successful To hit draws adds to the effect number of the weapon, BUT ONLY IF the weapon would hit on a Black 0  (i.e. its range is 0, 0-1, 0-2, etc.)  (Exceptions:  AT (boxed) ordnance from AFV's, IG's and ATR add the Relative Range, not the To Hit number if they hit.)

So a Russian Mortar at RR0, hits on 1 it's effect number is never modified--it will remain a 2.  

However at RR2 its To Hit Range is 0-2, it will have its Effect modified by +1 to 3 if a 1 was drawn or by +2 to 4 if a 2 was drawn on the To Hit draw.

The reasoning for this is that a single To Hit number indicates target that is hard to hit, any hit.  But if a range of numbers, it is possible to not only hit it, but hit right on the nose and do more damage.

ground_truth_answer:
Let me know if I'm understanding the rules right...

If I play a Wire card on my moving opponent's group and he rejects it, his movement card is placed sideways AND his chit range is taken back one? If so does this really just simply make him loose a step concerning movement? What would other benefits be? 

Let's start with this:  Wire cannot be rejected by an opponent.  Technically Wire is not a terrain card--so it can be discarded onto a moving or non-moving opposing group.  

If discarded onto a moving opposing group that group remains moving.  The opponent cannot play a terrain card (except Open Ground--which would stop the group from moving) on the group until the wire is removed.

What you describe is rejecting terrain.  When terrain is rejected, the last movement is modified:
-  If advancing or retreating, turn the Movement card sideways and the adjust the range chit to its previous value.
-  If the movement card was played sideways, remove it.  The group is no longer moving (if the final movement card was removed) and back in the original terrain.  Any advantage from that movement is also lost:  Flanking fire, group transfer, ford a stream.

Certain terrain cannot be rejected:  Stream, Minefield (non-desert), Marsh in a Jungle scenario, Soft Sand/Wadi in Desert scenario.

As to why does terrain get rejected is your opponent played a terrain you didn't want on the group to go into:   often a Marsh, sometimes you want to put them in a particular terrain like Buildings (see scenario B--City Fight) and your opponent offers you a Brush.  The effect on movement is the cost for rejecting the terrain.  

PS: I do know about him NOT qualifying for any flanking fire or lateral group transfers. 

As stated above, that group was moving sideways in both of those situations, the movement card was removed and any advantages were lost.

It is clearly clear the OP was confused--hence the question.

28.71:  Refers to the attacks specified in 28.7.

raw_question:
Hi all. Going to run this delicate rules problem by the Group here and see what's Your take on it.

A Group is in an unforded Stream, at relative range to an enemy Group in buildings. One man of the Group sucessfully fords, infiltrates and subsequently infiltrates the enemy Group, killing the last enemy in CC.

Now, rule 20.8 says:Whenever the last man in a Group is eliminated while his Group is infiltrated, the Terrain card his Group occupied (including entrenchments)n is subject to capture by any Group currently infiltrating that Group.

While rule 8.53 says: A Stream can be left only by fording.

Which rule takes presedence? Fording has occured, yes, but only by one man. So how is this going to go down?

R. :)
ground_truth_answer:
This was with me ... and at times, one has to put on their ASL rules hat, and then see things clearly clear.

As Brent Pollock above posted, if this was ASL, it would be easy to solve.  The ASL Rule Book clearly states, when there is a conflict between rules, the higher order rule number takes precedence.  We don't have that luxury in UF.  Additionally, there is no official Q&A mechanism anymore, such as MMP who have the rights to ASL now.  So we are left with the rule book and ourselves.

Indeed Rule 8.53’s first sentence does state “A Stream can only be left by fording.”  The first sentence of 8.53 needs to be read in context with the rest of paragraph 8.53.  Not as a stand-alone sentence to laser in on.  The rule discusses one way of how a GROUP moves off a Stream.  And yes, "a Stream can only be left by fording."  How? Continue to read the next sentence.  It plays a Movement card and draws a black RNC or a Movement card that is also a ford.  The rule is discussing how a Group can move off a Stream.

And of course, as others have pointed out, Stream is Terrain.  And 20.8 lists another way to acquire new Terrain through CC.  And Rule 20.24 lists the extra requirements to enter CC if you're in a Stream.

If I've satisfied the requirements of 20.24, I can now apply 20.8 and make my choice.  The first sentence of Rule 8.53 is not in play, as this is not a movement action for the Group, rather it is a CC action.

And as Richard Irving points out, I do agree with the Wire discussion.  First, it is Artificial Terrain.  Second, 13.34 when read in the entire context of the rule citation does limit placement of Terrain at any time (including CC).  There is no correlation of 13.34 to 8.53 however.  The "mandatory" portion of 8.53 is mandatory in respect to 8.53, which means when a group wishes to move off a Stream, they can do so only by Fording, which means to play of a Movement card on THAT Group in Sideways mode.  

I’m glad that I can contribute to the group.

query:
Close Combat on Wire: Just wanted to explore what happens when one of the involvees in Close Combat is on Wire: specifically, whether there is a -1 modifier to the CCV.

Firstly, how can this situation occur?  In four ways:

1) Most commonly, when the defender (ie the infiltrated group) is on Wire.

2) When the attacker infiltrates and then receives Wire while still infiltrating [13.36].

3) When the attackers are a Japanese Banzai group [45.423].  Note that this definitely states that the Banzai group, if on Wire, gets a -1 to CCV.

4) A Berserk man [20.91].  A clarification says: Berserk status allows CC in situations not normally allowed (i.e. vs. Pillbox or Minefield or from a Pillbox, Wire, Stream or Marsh). No infiltration check is made, and there is no modification made nor any check taken due to terrain or artificial terrain situations.

It’s worth noting that section 13.3 Wire talks about modifications to Fire Strength (or To Hit# for ordnance) but doesn’t mention modifications to CC.

So on the face of it we have no effect of Wire on CC except for Banzai men.

However, consider an argument from realism (I know, I know…), CC is combat at less than 50 yards, so includes close-range firefights and grenades as well as bayonet-and-knuckleduster stuff.  Wire is an abstraction of any condition that makes a group more vulnerable and/or less able to deliver fire; it seems to me perfectly justifiable to apply at least one of the modifiers to the CCV.

On that basis one could say that the references to Fire Strength in 13.32 should have included CCV; and that the exception for a Berserk attacker is reasonable because by definition he is unaware of his surroundings and thus ignoring any limitations imposed by Wire (look, he’s running around in a Minefield or battering at the slot of a Pillbox, so a few strands of wire aren’t going to inhibit him).

But what does the team think?

query:
AFV Questions: Yes to both questions.

28.43 BUTTONED UP: 
Any other AFV whose Morale defense value is equaled or exceeded by any attack becomes Buttoned Up when it is flipped over. An AFV which Buttons Up remains Buttoned Up for the duration of the scenario (barring play of a Hero card) whether it Buttons Up voluntarily or due to enemy fire. A Buttoned Up AFV functions normally in all respects, but tends to have poorer accuracy, firepower, and mobility qualities as a consequence. An AFV starts CE. Should it wish to Button Up voluntarily, it must expend an Action doing so.   

28.431 COMMANDER KILLED: 

If the AFV's MORALE defense value is <= the final attack result number, the AFV merely Buttons Up or is Pinned as stated in [28.4]. If, however, the final attack result number is also >= the Crew Exposed (CE) value (or a Sniper KIA has occurred), the AFV commander has been killed and the AFV suffers other penalties in addition to being Pinned/Buttoned Up. Place a Commander Killed chit on the AFV card. Henceforth, that ordnance will have its To Hit frequency and Overrun strength reduced by one, and any non-ordnance attack it makes will suffer a reduction of one to its Fire Strength.   
28.4311 

An OT AFV may conceivably suffer a Commander Killed result more than once because when it is rallied it is again CE. Should such an AFV suffer a second Commander Killed result, flip the Commander Killed chit over to the "2 Crew Killed" side. Its To Hit frequency is reduced by two, and any non-ordnance attack it makes will suffer a reduction of two to its Fire Strength. If an OT AFV suffers a third Commander Killed result it is eliminated.
28.4312 
Each Commander Killed result on an AFV also serves as a one column shift to the left when checking for infiltration against an AFV.

14.31 VS AFV:

No, this flow chart chart at best confusing and is wrong.

You probably should calculate the needed To Hit number before drawing the RNC:
-  To Hit is spectrum that looks like this:

0-6   0-5  0-4   0-3   0-2   0-1   0   1   2   3   4   5   6
+1 means go one to the left, -1 go one to the right

-  Start at the To Hit # at the weapon's range.
+1 for the weapon has acquired the target.
-X for a concealed card played
-1 for each smoke (IN or OUT) or Wire (Out)
Only Black RNC will hit if either target or firer is moving or target is hull down.  (If target AND firer are moving (or target hull down and firer moving) the RNC must be Black and an additional -1 TH is applied.) 

Then draw the card to check the RNC.

The chart has the RNC drawn first.  If it red, checks firer or target moving and if not still applies the -1 TH which is wrong.  It should ask if "Either target or firer are moving?".  If Yes, then ask "Is the RNC Black?". if No, shunt that off to a Miss.

query:
Things I Have Played Wrong For Years …: …until I used Bruce Wigdor’s Up Front program.  I keep spotting mistakes in the program and I used to report them to Bruce, until I got wise.  Now I check the UF rulebook first, and four times out of five I find I was wrong instead.  Here are a couple of completely obvious things that I’ve got wrong any time these last thirty years:

1) You can’t reverse a Flank.  If you have a Flanked group and you play a Flank card sideways, yes it breaks the Flank but nooooo you don’t get to flank the flankers.  There it is in black and white [17.2]: A group cannot laterally flank a group which currently enjoys a Flanking Fire advantage over it.

(Note: there are obscure exceptions involving Natural Flanking, before Richard points this out.)

2) If you have a group on a Hill firing on an enemy group on another Hill, what’s the Fire modifier?  Zero you say, +1 cancels the -1.   Nope.  The attacking group doesn’t get Elevated Fire against the target because they’re on a Hill – but the target does get the -1 for the Hill.  So it’s -1. [Edit: Actually this is wrong and I was right all along - see below.]

[8.31] A group occupying a Hill may use Elevated Fire [6.41] to add one to the Fire Strength of any attack they make against any target group not occupying another Hill or a Pillbox.

(Note the Pillbox bit as well – that’s easy to miss.)

I found this out when my Panzerschreck (on a Hill) hit a T-34 (also on a Hill, after the retreating Russians despicably drew a black 6 for Random Reinforcements) with a black 0, and scored a black 1 for effect.  Yes! I thought, 4+1=5, immobilised!  But no, it was -1 for the Hill so I was thwarted.  I’d actually have been better off if the Panzerschreck hadn’t been on a Hill, because then the T-34 would have been Hull Down, but the black 0 would still have hit and the -1 for the Hill wouldn’t have counted … except that of course you can’t get an immobilise result if the AFV is Hull Down. (It would have been Stunned: [28.93]: A Hull Down AFV or IG cannot be immobilized; an immobilization result is treated as a stun result instead.)

Funny, I didn’t realise you could immobilise an IG ….

(In case you were wondering, I managed to win when Bernhoff, the last survivor of his 6-man group, snatched up the flamethrower and used a 1/5 Fire card to kill the one man I needed to get a break – possibly the worst Fire card ever used to win a scenario.)

query:
Lateral Group Transfer & Individual Transfer Oddities: Hi all

Had a game with my son last night (yay!) and he raised an interesting question about lateral transfers.

Basically he wondered why it was relatively simple to shift a whole group sideways but relatively hard (and super dangerous for the transferring soldier) to move single men between two groups.

Plus there's the thing where two entire groups can swap IDs by simultaneously moving past each other sideways...but if they want to merge into a single group they have to do it man by man..?

And then there's the other thing where a group consisting of a single guy  would suffer +1 to incoming fire when he's moving...but if that same soldier tried to transfer into another group he'd effectively get penalised for moving by...+2..?

I'm not arguing for house rules or anything of that sort, and I can see the gameplay requirement for this (you probably don't want single men leaping around the battlefield with gay abandon, or new groups forming or splitting up too simply and regularly). The thing is, most of Up Front's seeming weirdness actually makes perfect sense in its own terms but this area puzzles me. So I was wondering - is there something historical/practical that all this lateral movement funkiness might be simulating?

Any thoughts? :)

G

ground_truth_answer:
I worried about it early on but long ago gave up. Every game I have ever played has had at least one head scratching moment; this has always been it for me. I love the game despite this quirk.

The other quirk is been relative range counting up. Would have Ben easy to do it the other way, but it is easy to resolve. It just looks funny.

The ill-fated kickstarter version was to have distance the following formula:

Distance = 5 - (Sum of Range Chits)
  Use Absolute value if >0  (i.e. |-1| = 1), 
  Adding 1 for lateral distance (i.e. more a single letter apart), 
  Max value of 5 for firing purposes

Advantages:
-  Makes 0 = close, 5 = far away.

Disadvantages:
Some game rules become really complicated:
-  Retrograde:  Moving to Distance >5 to nearest group is prohibited, etc.

-  Firing boxed ordnance from AFV/IG:  Currently add RR to effect.  under these rules you'd have to subtract it (also Boxed Effect Number of every weapon would need to be modified.)

-  Night scenarios:  Currently observation is done by drawing an RNC:  0-RR = sighted enemy and can fire at it.  With distance, it becomes 0 - (5-distance)

-  

The only silver lining about that KS failing is that it didn't allow them to screw up the rules like this. In the same vein, I'm happy to have the original cards with the weapons printed on them instead of the weapons as chits system.

query:
Group Creation using Open Ground: Here’s an obscure question – or rather a straightforward question where the answer is obscure.  During play, you can create a new group by making an Individual Transfer of two or more men simultaneously from an existing group, and subsequently putting them into terrain, either by playing a Terrain card on them or by accepting your opponent’s discard of a Terrain card.  The question is, can you create the new group by playing an inverted card as Open Ground?

At first sight one would say yes, of course, and this is how I’ve always played (on the rare occasions that this has arisen).  But playing Bruce Wigdor’s program recently I noticed that it doesn’t allow it – you have to play a “proper” Terrain card.  I was going to point this out as a bug, but I’ve several times reported bugs only to have Bruce point out kindly but firmly that I haven’t got the rules quite right, so I thought I’d check.  And on doing so, I began to wonder …

The relevant rule is 17.92:

The Group Creation is completed when the new group plays a Terrain card. If any transferring man is pinned prior to the play of a Terrain card on its group -- the transfer fails and the entire group is returned to the creating group. Otherwise, all rules for Individual Transfer apply.

OK, so an Open Ground card is a Terrain card, surely?  Let’s see what the rules say about playing Terrain cards; in 5.1 we have:

A Terrain card may be placed on any group (even one containing pinned Personality cards) provided it already has a Movement card of some type in place which is not already covered by another Terrain or Wire card.

So that’s the “proper” Terrain cards.  The use of Open Ground cards is covered in 8.1:

The back of every Action card depicts Open Ground. …  A player wishing to move into Open Ground may do so by playing any card face down on top of an already placed Movement card.

That covers normal movement, but in the Group Creation situation of course there isn’t an “already placed” Movement card.  So technically, I suppose, you can’t do it.  (And as usual, Bruce’s program accurately reflects the rules as written.)

From a realism point of view this doesn’t makes much sense – if you can start a group in Open Ground, or bring reinforcements into Open Ground, surely you should be able to create a new group in Open Ground.  You could make a case, perhaps, for saying that men would be unwilling to leave the perceived safety of an existing group unless there was some cover for them to leap into – although the rules would allow you to put them in a Stream.

So I think this is a case where the rules don’t quite say what they mean – shock, horror.  In framing 8.1 the writer forgot to allow for the obscure case we’re talking about.  But what does the Up Front world at large think?

ground_truth_answer:
When playing a card that must be played as a discard (wire, sniper, etc.), does the pplayer discard that card as part of his normal discard for his nationality, or does that single card play replace the normal discard procedure?

For example, if the Russian player discards a sniper, is he still allowed to discard the rest of his hand (or any part of it) as well?

You can play a Sniper, Wire, terrain an opposing moving group and/or discard up to the number allowed by your nationality:  1 for German, French, 2 for British, Japanese, Italian, American, all for Russians.

In addition:
-  Russians may attempt entrenchment one or more times in lieu of a discard for each attempt.

Nope. Discarding a sniper on one group and discarding a wire on another group would count as their two discards.

ground_truth_answer:
I introduced the game to a friend today (talk about the blind guiding the blind... )

We were pushing on opposite sides of the groups, I moved Group A from the Gully in Range 3 to Range 4 and he moved from a woods in range 3 to Range 4. In my turn I didn't have a terrain card for the win, so I threw a wire to his units in range 4.

According to the rules I have seen he can play a terrain card below a Wire (no problem with that) and he wins if the card terrain plus (minus) the wire is above 1. But is it with the wall? Several  problems here:
-  Terrain under wire:  Except for open ground, you cannot play terrain on a moving group in wire.  The play of the wall is illegal so long as the wire is there. (see 13.34 & 13.5)

-  Modifications to TEM for victory conditions:   Yes, Wire/Entrenchments count for determining "terrain that with reduce the Fire Strength  of an attack against them."  

In the case of a Wall, one wire on top of it does NOT completely nullify the reduction capability even if there is no directly opposite group.  Two wire cards on a wall would invalidate the Wall for this VC.  

Smoke does NOT count for this purpose--because breeze could blow it away.  (16.421)

These VC's have 5 parts:
-  X or more unpinned men.  (Pinned men don't count.)
-  in one of more groups  (They do not all have to be in the same group)
-  non-infiltrated (i.e. if a group is infiltrated the men in that group cannot count for the VC.)
-  at the proper Range Chit or Relative Range  (and not more)
-  In terrain that will reduce the fire effect of an attack against it.
All 5 parts have to exist to claim victory.

This means pinning some guys or infiltrating the group can be an effective last ditch way of staving off a loss.

2 {Points:
-  The minefield is a type of terrain--as soon as a group enters terrain, the previous movement cards and prior terrain are placed in the discard pile.  The movement/terain cards on the group would be:

Move
Move, Move
Minefield,
Minefield, Move
Minefield Move, Move.

So the prior movement cards were already gone before you were fired on.
-  Only the last two Movement or terrain cards count.  There can only be  movements cards OR (last movement card+last terrain) OR {Last terrain and no movement) + any Smoke or Wire cards vcan ever apply.

So correct, in your situation, the Defensive TEM would +2 since two movements cards are in play regardless of the terrain card below them (There is an exception for Gully)  

- Close combat. One of my Russian units (in wire) got berserk and attack an opposing enemy unit. I randomly selected the defender in a 4 man group. Now, what is the modifier? Is it +9 (+3 per man that is not being attacked) or 0 (because the +3 only enters play when you attack a manned weapon)?

The +3 modifier applies only:
-  When the attacking players has multiple men assigned to the same CC target.
-  When defending in CC, the the man selected is part of a multiman crew.
See 20.71 & 20.622.

Unless the Berserker was a attacking a crewed MG, the CC would be his PINNED value with no modification.

ground_truth_answer:
I am learning (slowly, very slowly) how to play this game and I came into a question that I am not sure how to resolve.

What happens when a group is only 1 unit big, or when a group has disappeared?

In my case, Russian Group B was hit hard (more on that later) by a German attack and ended up with 1 soldier left and the soldier was pinned (yes it was bad).

That sort of stuff happens.

What happens to a 1 unit group? I played as if nothing happened but I remember reading something about groups being at least 2 units strong.

One man in a group is still a group.  Only at the start of play or if a group is created by individual transfer during play does it have to be a minimum of 2 men.

Afterwards the germans infiltrated and killed the Russian in Close Combat (I am learning so this was part of the learning process), they took the terrain (scenario B and the terrain was a building), and now I have a Russian Group A, and a Russian Group C. What should I do?

Lack of a Group B is not a problem.  The Russian can "group transfer" (i.e. move sideways) either A or C to refill B, but they are not required to. 

All that happens when a group is eliminated is any terrain/movement card (unless the terrain is captured by the opponent) is discarded and the group ID & range chits are removed.

BTW, I am finding that this game is very bloody. An attack of 0 can easily pin a couple of guys (morale 2 or even 3),

A fire strength attack of 0 will pin a Morale 2 man about 1/4 of the time (~41/162), Morale 3 man about 1/6 of the time  (~27/162)  Morale 2 is a pretty weak guy.  

A Fire 0 attack against against a 6 man group might pin a man or not.  Placing the low morale guys where they are less likley to be targeted is a key part of the strategy of the game. 

 and routing them afterwards is very easy if they are moving, 
It should be noted that a group with pinned men can't have a movement  card played on it, even to remove wire.  (It is possible for there to be pinned men in a moving group, but they have to have started moving first and then were pinned by a later attack.) 

and you have to move in this game. I suppose that once I learn more rules things will change but I am mostly winning scenarios (against myself) by staying put and shooting everyone from afar.

You can't move willy-nilly, you have to prepare to move:
-  Don't advance without having a concealment and/or a rally card and a terrain card in your before playing the Move.
-  It is less risky to advance from good defensive terrain. 
-  Play a smoke on a group (if you can) before moving it.
-  Don't advance until your opponent's firebase has had some men pinned (particularly if the LMG is pinned)
-  If you are playing the Russian or Japanese or Italians who have no rifle FP at RR1, time your advance when the opposing firebase advances.

Of course late in the game, you may have no choice.

That being said, novice players tend to advance too rashly.  Three decks is quite a bit of time.

ground_truth_answer:
1. What is the significance of a card with an underlined name (such as Russian #38 SU-85)? I didn't think much of it until I read the errata file in the File section and it mentioned that some British cards should have their names underlined.

Underlined AFV's are assault guns which do not have a rotating turret.  (28.2)  In game terms, assault guns have -1 TH vs. moving target, -2TH when bogged or immobilized, and cannot fire when moving.

2. When a card specifies availability with only one date (a year or a month-year like Russian card #34 T34b, available 7/1941), does that mean it's available during that year or half-year only, or is it available beginning from that time until the end of the war?

It is available to the end of the war--but you probably should "phase out" early war equipment if you are designing an historically accurate late war scenario.

3. Russian card #38 (the SU-85 again...you can see which cards I've been looking at today) has one special rule on the front (No Moving Fire Allowed) and two different special rules on the back (+1 TH vs Moving, +2 TH if Bogged/Immobilized). Do all three rules apply to the AFV regardless of CE/Buttoned Up status, or do they only apply to the CE/Buttoned Up status on the side of the card on which they're printed?

The SU-85 is an assault gun.  All assault guns have those notes--with the except of the French 34 Char B1-bis 75mm Hull gun--which is treated as an assault gun.  Those rules apply whether buttoned up or not.  

3b. If the SU-85 is Bogged, it gets a +2 TH. I assume this is supposed to be a penalty, which now makes it harder to hit a target, so I would add +2 to all the TH numbers at any given range. When the TH number is printed originally as a range (0-2), that turns it into a 2-4 required to hit, right?

It is best to think of To Hit numbers in a spectrum, the left is better than the right:

0-6   0-5   0-4   0-3   0-2   0-1   0   1   2   3   4   5   6 

Bonuses and penalties are applied by moving left or right the appropriate number of steps.  (see 25.6)

AH was inconsistent with how it expressed TH bonus/penalties:
-  For acquisition, "+1TH" means to improve the TH number by moving to the left on the above chart.
-  For assault guns,  "+1TH" means to penalize you moving to the right.  (Which kind of makes sense in harder shots as TH1 is penalized to TH2.) 
-  Stream and Wire, "-1TH" means a penalty for firing a panzerfaust or fully crewed, non-moving, ordnance weapon (in Stream).
-  Concealment Cards/Smoke:  -1 means to make the shot harder, i.e. to the right.

Now that I think about it, I didn't catch that when I proofread the Banzai/Desert War cards  :gulp:.  At least it is obvious when penalty or bonus is to be applied.

4. Conceptually, what does Hull Down represent? I've read the rules and I'm still having a hard time visualizing what is happening to the AFV when it is Hull Down.

Some posted a nice chart showing the concept.  Essentially, the AFV is partially blocked so in game terms, a red TH is a miss.

ground_truth_answer:
No - what it means is that when either group is fired at, the man in question is one of the targets and he (only) gets an additional +2 Fire modifier.

So if Group A is entrenched in Woods and Group B is entrenched on a Hill under Wire, and Private Gormless transfers from A to B:

Fire against Group A is at -3, except for Gormless who is at 0 (Woods -2, entrench doesn't count for Transferring, +2 for Transferring).

Fire against Group B is at -1 (Hill -1, Entrench -1, Wire +1) except for Gormless, who is at +2 (Hill +1, Wire -1, entrench doesn't count, transferring +2).

Note also that the man transferring in or out is fired on first.
I think you mean "Hill -1, Wire +1" in Gormless' example B, but otherwise, I understand what you mean. Thanks.

query:
The rules that most need refining?: What are they, if any, in your mind?

I have two.

Weapon Malfunctions:
I don't see the need for all the exceptions.  I say whatever position you draw that persons weapon malfunctions, no matter what.  Now if it was a weapon that wasn't capable of contributing to the fire mission than the fire strength isn't modified.  If it is (even ones that currently have a 0 at the current range, the soldiers may be firing just ineffective) than the fire mission is modified in the usual way.

Inf./CC:
I'm fine with it being a two step process.  I just think it burns way too many cards.  

I'd like to come up with a way to determine Inf and CC matchups with just one card each.  I've been pondering the possibility but it would probably significantly change the odds, which I don't know if that's for the good.

Without putting too much thought into it here's possibly a way.  The number and the color are used to determine inf. 19.13     If the firing group contains more than one weapon with usable firepower factors, a RPC is immediately drawn to determine which weapon in the group actually malfunctions. All weapons in an attacking group (even those with a firepower of 0) are considered to be firing when the group attacks (EXC: flamethrowers, secondary weapons, ordnance, non-firing infiltrators, and the weapons of designated crewmen). If the RPC indicates a non-firing weapon has malfunctioned, there is no effect. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a pinned man, there is no effect to the attack, but the pinned man's weapon does malfunction. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a designated assistant crewman of a firing MG or a man whose weapon has no firepower at its current range, the malfunction is considered only momentary, and the fire against any remaining defenders in the defending group yet to be attacked is resolved with one less Fire Strength, but no weapon malfunctions. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a firing weapon, that weapon malfunctions and combat vs. any remaining defenders not yet fired upon is resolved with one less Fire Strength for every two Firepower factors (or fraction thereof) previously contributed by the malfunctioned weapon. This reduction to the Fire Strength is made after any halving effects for Moving or Night Fire, and is made even if the firing group did not require that weapon's firepower in order to play the Fire card(s) used in the attack.

19.14     Although pinned men and those with already malfunctioned weapons are not considered to be firing, their weapons are always subject to malfunction (including flamethrower, ordnance, and the principal weapon of a designated crewman). A player cannot specify men as not firing solely to avoid the possibility of their weapons malfunctioning.

So, if zero firepower, it malfunctions, but you just lose one fire strength as a penalty.  No malfunction chit.

If pinned man, (they are scared so firing without purpose), they DO get a malfunction chit.

Two problems with this theory:
-  It is possible (and not particularly unlikely) that a player with more VP's could have a squad break. 

Example: In Scenario A:
Germans:  4 men at RC3 + 4 KIA's = 20 VP's
Americans:  8 men at RC1 + 5 KIA's + 1 rout = 19 VP's

-  And specifically per 16.4, VP's only apply at the end of a scenario "at the end of the time limit" and only those scenarios where the "which include a condition where one player wins by deny their opponent's Victory Conditions."

16.4 is VP's  

16.41 states pinned men & bogged/immobilized/pinned AFV's don;t count for VP's.
  
Then, 16.42 is about what count as terrain "that reduces the Fire Strength of an attack against them" (which does NOT apply for VP calculation.)  This should have been listed before VP's and should specify that certain VP's may terminate the game immediately when achieved. 

Then they get around the incomplete Squad Break rule in 16.5

They pick the least important and least common way to win and list it first and put a higher subhead on it.  :shake:  

To be fair to Courtney and Don, in 1983 they probably didn't have a word processor to quickly make changes during the editing process.  :)

The three reasons I think the rules are so bad:
-  They don't give a big picture view of how the game is played.  Here's the game looks when set up, here's how a player plays a turn, here how you use each particular card, etc.  
-  They fail as a reference because of Programmed Instruction, basically rules are listed in the order of which scenario they were introduced in. query: Japanese SNLF troops: Banzai 45.8 rule says that SNLF are Japanese second line troops. I'm guessin' why, considering that Advanced Squad Leader rulebook consider those troops roughly equivalent to the US Marine Corps. Just a thought.:)
title: Japanese SNLF troops
raw_question: Banzai 45.8 rule says that SNLF are Japanese second line troops. I'm guessin' why, considering that Advanced Squad Leader rulebook consider those troops roughly equivalent to the US Marine Corps. Just a thought.:)
ground_truth_answer:
SNLF are "Marines" in the sense they are part of the Navy, but their training and equipment was generally inferior to the Imperial Japanese Army.  (Unlike U.S. Marines)

Per the Designer Notes in Banzai:

Contrary to common belief, the SNLF were not superior to, or even equal to, normal troops.  Conversely , they exhibited a surprising lack of ability in infantry combat when encountering determined resistance.   In game terms, I have used then to represent almost any "second line" troops for convenience.  Take note as well, that there are no true elite troops listed for Japanese because there really weren't any.  Although there were units that performed exceedingly well in combat, that was due as much to circumstance or leadership as to organization.  The term "Samurai", which we use to classify elite units is merely a term of convenience; no such organized unit existed.

To a large extent, the names of elite and second line troops in Up Front for all nationalities are "terms of convenience".  Elite troops are used in scenarios for any experienced, highly trained, exceptional forces even if they aren't a part of of the "Guards", "Bersaglieri", "SS", "Airborne", etc.  (Note the Kickstarter edition, the name for the elite Germans was to be changed from "SS" to "Panzer Grenadier"--in large part due to SS troops not being superior, and often inferior, to regular Wehrmacht troops despite, or because of, their fanaticism.)  Likewise 2nd line troops, whether they are "conscripts", "Black shirts", "Volksgrenadiers", etc. are used for any troops with diminished effectiveness due to fatigue, replacements, etc.

I can never remember what the official names are and simply call then "Elite"______ or "second line" ______ troops :)

ground_truth_answer:
Rule 25.3 states that a Fire card of any value must be played for ordnance to make a To Hit attempt versus an AFV.  However, I'm a but confused by 28.31.

Rule 28.31 states, "If there are insufficient boxed firepower factors in a group to use a particular Fire card, the Armor and Flank defense values are not affected by an attack using that card."

28.31 is not referring an ordnance attack--it is referring to a "boxed firepower" attack.  

Most firepower in unboxed (like with rifles/machine guns, etc. and thus per 28.31 does not apply vs. the ARMOR/FLANK defense values of the AFV's (Though they would apply vs. CE/Button UP/Pinned values of an AFV.) 1) Your sniper is an abstract member of your squad right?  And you only have one unless the scenario says otherwise right?

The sniper might not be a member of your squad, but just in the area. In any case, you only have one unless the scenario or rules say otherwise. (14.4, 37.4, 43.6)

2) A group with a pinned members can still have a terrain card on them if they already have a movement card in play right?  For example, the German unit B plays a movement card.  Then on the American player's turn they fire on Group B and pins 3 members.  On the next German turn, I can play a woods on them right?

Correct. Pinned units may still play terrain cards if they have a valid movement card (see 5.1) (if they're fording a stream or getting out of a swamp, they may be stuck).

3)  How long do movement cards stay on their stacks?  Everything I've seen suggestions movement cards discard previous terrain (2 of them discard a stream).  Terrain discards previous movement cards.  Is that how it works?  The rule book makes it seem like the stack just stays on the group the whole game. Also, I can play any card on a movement card as open terrain.  This is to negate the fire bonus the opponent gets, no?

You discard all movement cards and terrain cards when a new terrain card is played (5.41). Otherwise they stay there.

However, you use at most two movement/terrain cards for determining fire modifiers. (7.2) - which will either be two movement cards, or a terrain and a movement card. (Wire or Smoke modifiers may be used in addition...)

ground_truth_answer:
One never loses VP as a result of taking casualties. One gains VP from eliminating or routing the opponent's forces.

If a man is removed from the game due to Rout, that's 1VP for the opponent. If a man is removed from the game via Panic or KIA, that's 2VP for the opponent. This, along with all other aspects of calculating one's VP total, is covered in rule 16.4.

Removal due to Panic is considered KIA for VP purposes as indicated in rule 6.53. Also note that if you choose to eliminate one of your own men via Voluntary Panic, you must draw an RPC to determine whether they Panic or Rout for enemy VP purposes, as per rule 10.3.

A group is in brush (-1) and has a move played on it (+1). Am I correct that the defensive fire modifier is 0? Is the group still considered to be in the brush, only moving? Basically, only the last two movement and/or "permanent" terrain cards are counted for terrain effect modifiers.  Everything in your example is correct except  terrain/move/move you only consider the two movement cards so it's a +2.  Terrain/move/move/move is also +2.

Also note technically, you do not discard movement or terrain until you enter new permanent terrain  *found in the errata) as it is possible to reject terrain multiple times and be forced back into the original terrain. 

A group is in a gully where they cannot be fired upon (some exceptions) and has a move played on it. Units still cannot fire on it (again there are exceptions). If another move card is played on them, they are still considered to be in the gully, but can now be fired upon at... -2 (gully) and +1 (move)? If they play a 3rd move, are they now in the open? What is the defensive fire modifier?

Nope.  Gullies are confusing, but the effect is NOT as as you describe:
The the firing group is  not on a Hill or at RR5, Gullies "hide" the first movement card played and  work as follows:
-  No move: can't be fired on
-  1 move:  can't be fired on (also moving group can now go into new terrain.  There is no exception that prevents terrain being played on a moving group in a gully.)
-  2 movements:  +1  (The terrain has no effect, but first move is considered to be "hidden" from the firer.  It is an exception to the "only last 2 movement/terrain cards count")
-  3 movements:  +2  (as per the "last two movement/terrain cards count" rule.)

If the firer is on a hill or at RR5, the defender gets a -2 TEM and there is no hidden movements, treat like any other terrain situation.  (Only last 2 movement/terrain count, etc.)

Scenario A requires units to be at "Range Chit 4" to win. I get it that if they have 4 moves played on them they will be there, but what if the opposing group is at range 2? Does that mean they cannot push to 4 without eliminating or otherwise pushing the enemy back to range 1 (since the max range is 5)?

You are ignoring one possibility-lateral movement (called "Group transfer" in the rules.)  This allows you move laterally changing Grouip B to Group C by declaring the start of the transfer when you play a sideways movement card and the completing the transfer when playing terrain on the group.  

This would allow bypassing an enemy group to reach range chit 4.

I have trouble understanding the above rule. I thought only open ground can be played beneath a smoke card and any terrain played above a smoke card will cancel it?
ground_truth_answer:
But if it discard the smoke beneath it, why would it adds to the defensive value of the last played terrain card?

And what is there to stop me from moving range 0 to range 5 in the cover of smoke simply by playing move, open ground, move, open ground.

I think you have a bit of a misunderstanding here - new cards aren't played or discarded beneath smoke cards which are already on the table. A terrain card played on a group which has smoke present is played above the smoke, and immediately gets rid of the smoke cards. You can't play a card beneath a smoke card which is already present on the table.

To move from 0 to 5 under cover of a single smoke card as you describe in the second paragraph therefore isn't possible. 

13.23. Smoke does not prevent a Terrain card from being played on a previously placed Movement card, it merely adds to the defensive value of the last played Terrain card beneath it in that group.

I have trouble understanding the above rule. I thought only open ground can be played beneath a smoke card and any terrain played above a smoke card will cancel it?

Referring to 'the last played terrain card beneath it' does not mean you can play a terrain card beneath previously placed smoke. It just refers to terrain cards which were present before the smoke card was played. I think this is the crux of your misunderstanding here.

Regarding 'only open ground can be played beneath a terrain card'. Any terrain card can be played on top of a smoke card, providing there is a movement card already present.

query:
What exactly is a 'turn'?: If I pin my opponent's SL and he rallys him on his turn does he still receive 1 less card?

If I fire and a breeze card appears can my opponent play smoke on his turn?
title: What exactly is a 'turn'?
raw_question:
If I pin my opponent's SL and he rallys him on his turn does he still receive 1 less card?

If I fire and a breeze card appears can my opponent play smoke on his turn?
ground_truth_answer:
If I pin my opponent's SL and he rallys him on his turn does he still receive 1 less card?

No.  If a player's SL (or ASL if the SL is eliminated) is pinned when he draws cards, he draws one fewer card.  If my opponent pins my SL and I rally him on the very next turn, I draw my full allotment of cards.

Also on the player's next turn after his SL is eliminated, a player always draws one fewer card--whether or not the ASL is punned.

If I fire and a breeze card appears can my opponent play smoke on his turn?
Yes.  Breeze only applies on the turn it was drawn.

A turn is one player's assigned of actions and ends with refilling his hand.

Later in the thread:
I suppose if it's near the end of the third deck and you already have the card or cards you need to win a sudden death victory. 

Actually you can always choose not refill your hand.  And you might choose to do so if you think the final deck will run out as you suggest.  No need to worry about whether SL/ASL is pinned or not.
