Ordinance: Hi Greg,

Yes, in this example you would score a hit by drawing 0-2, so your draw of 1 would result in a hit. The colour of the number would not matter, unless either yourself or your target were moving, in which case a red 0-2 would be a miss.

Your hit strength when using boxed effect numbers against AFVs is equal to the boxed effect number, plus a number equal to the relative range between firer & target (in this case 2). This would result in a hit strength of 7 + 2 = 9 in your example.

25.4 HIT STRENGTH: 
Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.) The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5].

If you are new to Up Front, I would advise starting with scenario 1 - a meeting of patrols, and wouldn't even think of attempting ordnance, let alone AFVs until you are familiar & comfortable with the rules for infantry, fire attacks, terrain effects, lateral group & individual transfer, infiltration, close combat, etc, etc. 

Take your time & learn to walk before you try to run - it will be worth it.

PS - the firepower adjacent to the range is used when the AFV fires its machine gun at a target rather than using its main ordnance weapon.

ground_truth_answer:
The ordnance rules do make sense once you understand what they are trying to represent.  There are two distinct cases: firing high explosive (HE) and armour piercing (AP) – solid shot.  In both cases, whether or not you hit uses the same process – you have to draw less than or equal to the To Hit number.

1) With HE, the important thing is how close to the target the hit is.  This is represented by getting a higher draw (but still within the to Hit number).  So if you are hitting on “0-3”, a 2 is a “closer” hit than a 0.  To represent this, the 2 is added to the HE (unboxed) effect against each target.  If your To Hit is low enough that it’s less than “0”, for example a “1”, you’re never going to get a really close hit, so you don’t get to add the 1 if you do hit.  On the other hand, if you have a high To Hit, eg “0-4”, you are fairly certain to hit, and have decent chance of getting a better hit by drawing a positive number – which increases your effect.

2) With AP, which is only used against AFVs, it’s different.  By making a successful To Hit draw, you’ve already hit the vehicle, and the question is whether you penetrate it – where you hit is comparatively unimportant (it’s assumed you hit on the front of the target – if you get a flank/rear shot the target usually has lower defence values to represent this).  What affects the likelihood of penetration is how close the firing ordnance is to the target.  So in this case you add the relative range to the AP (boxed) effect number of the ordnance.  For example, if you are both at Range 0, the RR is 0, so you add nothing.  If you’ve moved forward to Range 1 and he is at Range 2, the RR is 3, so you add 3.

In both cases, having evaluated the final Hit Strength, you check the final effect for each target (eg each man in a group targeted by HE) by drawing an RNC and use the red/black number, subtracting or adding the value to give the final effect.  For an AP shot there will never be more than one target, but you still do this final check by turning a single card.

Bear in mind that when firing ordnance against a AFV which is not buttoned up or pinned (open-topped AFVs are pinned rather than buttoning-up) you can choose whether to fire HE or AP – with HE you are trying to hit the exposed crew and force them to close down, or if you’re lucky, get a Commander Killed result.  In this case you use the normal HE procedure as above.

There are some ordnance weapons which don’t have a choice between HE and AP – they only ever fire one or the other.  So mortars only ever fire HE.  ATRs only ever fire AP, although they have an alternative use as a kind of infantry rifle with 1 FP.  Bazookas, panzerfausts, panzerschrecks and PIATs are firing a shaped charge whose effect is less predictable than solid shot, so there is a random element in calculating their effect, and they do use the HE procedure when firing against an AFV, even though the final result is compared to the AFV’s armour defence value.

And finally, just for completeness, some early war British AFVs didn’t carry HE ammunition, so they are confined to firing solid shot against infantry targets.  This is represented by using the HE procedure, but never adding a bonus to their unboxed Hit Strength of 0 even when they get a “close” hit.  So you can land a 6-pdr (57mm) solid shot among an infantry group and maybe scare them, but you’re unlikely to kill anyone!

Questions: Terrain cards might stop movement. If you play a terrain card on your own moving group, the group stops moving. If your opponent discards a terrain card on your group, you can choose to accept the terrain (and thus stop moving) or you can change the movement card you have in play to sideways (reducing your current range-chit again). If the movement card was already played sideways and you choose to reject it, the movement card is instead removed.

A wire-discard on your moving group doesn't stop movement, but you cannot enter terrain (except open ground) or play another movement card to change range until you have played a movement card to remove the wire.

R.:)

Can you place wire on an individual transfer?  The rules say wire is placed on a moving group.  It doesn't specifically mention an individual moving though.

Yes, wire can be placed. It would be placed on either the transferring or receiving group. It would affect fire against that group, including the transferring man (who is subject to fire against both groups until transfer is complete), but would not hinder or disrupt the transfer.

17.8 Before an Individual Transfer is completed, the opponent places wire on the "sending" group. Since the Transfer was begun when the sending group had no wire, can the transfer still be completed?

If I understand your scenario, the play is perfectly legal. There is no restriction based on RR against discarding terrain on an opposing group. And there is no limitation based on RR on accepting or rejecting terrain discarded on one of your groups.

1. Russian a0 moves up to a1(move fwd).
2. German A0 moves back to A-1(move retro) and discards Marsh on a1(move fwd).
3. Russian may now accept the Marsh and stop in a1(marsh) OR reject Marsh and change to a0(move side).
4. Russian rejects Marsh, changes to a0(move side). a0 plays a Wall and becomes a0(Wall).
5. German plays Woods and becomes A-1(Woods).

a0 and A-1 are at RR-1, but for all fire/TH purposes, they are considered to be at RR0.

Neither a0 nor A-1 can now play a retro Move card because of 5.51 which says a unit may not RETREAT if it will DECREASE the RR between it and the CLOSEST group TO < 0. The RR is already < 0 due to other legal plays, including a legal retreat played when the groups were AT RR1 after the Russian's advance.

If there were a Russian group in b3 now, German A-1 could retreat again to A-2, because the closest group (b3) is currently at RR2, regardless of whether Russian a is at 0 or -10.

Assuming you mean the RPC (Random Position Card) and generally used to select 1 man out of X men in the group for event like Sniper or weapon malfunction & infiltration.  So if there are 7 men in the group, you look at the number 7.

Some RPC numbers are used in specific situation which are marked by letters;

-  Cclose combat vs.AFV's:  2b if used to attack a "buttoned up AFV", 4c to attack "Commander Exposed AFV", 5o for "Open Topped AFV's"  (This menas it easier to attack a buttoned up AFV.

  What exactly does 5.7 mean? In order to move further forawrd, the opposite group whose Range chit blocks a further advance would have to retreat or be eliminated. Does this mean you just can not move until the group opposite is eleminated or moves back? 

When two groups are at RR5 to each other, they are are in the same area within about 15m each other.  Two groups with the same ID letter  (i.e. in the same column) cannot pass through each other.  So in order to advance further in the same column, the opposing group in the same column must either move back to allow you to move forward or the opposing group must be eliminated.  

Concealed: Does this mean you have to remember who already shot and this group can never be concealed again?

Nope.  Concealment lasts for single fire attack.  So if I fire at you from group A and you play a Concealment--the both the Fire cards, Concelment card and all RNC cards used to resolve the attack are immediately discarded.   If I then fire from Group B on the same group on the same turn or a later turn, the previous Concealment card has no effect.  You would have to play another Concealment card (if you had one), to reduce the fire.

A common tactic is fire is to fire from two groups on the same turn, hoping the first smaller attack will draw out a concealment card so the larger second attack can done at maximum strength.

Moving is the dangerous thing that can be done on a battlefield.  You generally do not want to move unless you have to or if you some sort of cover:  the enemy group mostly pinned or stuck in wire, a good conceal card or terrain card in hand.  

You have to spend many turns discarding, getting rid of cards you have no use for at the moment to hope getting ones you can use now.

ground_truth_answer:
RedGroup at RR1, BlueGroup at RR4 
Total RR is 5

Assuming two things:
-  Red and Blue are opposing sides--which you never say.  Who the hell are "red" and "blue"?
-  That they are directly opposite (i.e. both have the same Group letter) or adjacent groups (one letter's difference).  If one was Group A and the other Group C or D or E, then the RR is adjusted by -1 to RR4.

For less confusion, express a group's position "Range 1" or "Range Chit 4" or RC4.  Use RR only to express the relative position between two groups. Red is at RC1 and Blue is at RC4.

Also any two directly opposite or adjacent enemy groups whose range chit total equals 5 are at RR5:  1 vs. 4, 2 vs. 3, 5 vs. 0, -1 vs. 6, etc.

Redgroup has infiltrated and engaged in CloseCombat and eliminated all
of BlueGroup
The groups must be at RR5 to each other in order to engage in CC at all.  

You must be at RR5 to establish infiltration and keep it if the opposing group moves to RR4 until that group places terrain, but you cannot enter CC unless the groups are at RR5.

Redgroup can now take Bluegroups TerrainCard if desired
Yes, they can now capture the opposing groups terrain if they wish.  In fact during each close combat, the winning man (if any) can capture any of the losing man weapons.  

ExBluegroups RR4 chit is removed from play..
Redgroup remains at RR1 (with whichever terrain card prefered)

The eliminated group no longer exists so their so their range chit is removed from play.  The eliminating group, even if they choose top capture terrain, remains at whatever range chit they are at.

ground_truth_answer:
Hmmm, I'm not sure about that. I tend to take the original stance from the ASL game which always said "Don't focus on what the rules DON"T say, but what they do say." In this case, I might tend to cap the F.P. off at x3.

Where in the rules can this be justified?  You say one thing, yet doing another.

There is no rule anywhere that says FP is limited to x3. 

 Nevertheless, a very good question and your logic seems completely sound to me Bob. I must admit though, your second statement made me laugh about "deserving what happens" :)

There are rules that say that FP is doubled when infiltrating, flanking and having a Hero card played on a man and a note saying that in the case of a Hero only that "If the man is already entitled to double firepower, triple it instead."  (For argument's sake, the Hero doubles the uncrewed FP of crewed weapon, but neither flanking nor infiltration have this restriction, so you can't argue consistency.)

Clearly there are several reasonable interpretations (which may be covered in the errata--but I can't check since the website is down):
-  Each FP doubling could be implied to add one to the multiplier in each case, therefore x4.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as adding one multiplier to the final modifier, therefore x5.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as converting one of these doublings to a tripling, therefore x6.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause doesn't say anything anything about already quadrupled FP, so it doubles FP again:  therefore x8.
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as converting each of these doublings to a tripling, therefore x9
-  FP is doubled for flanking and then doubled again for infiltration, the the Hero clause is interpreted as not applying at all (It says doubled FP is tripled, but does not say anything about higher multipliers.) therefore x4 (Yes, it is same result as the first case, but a completely different reasoning.)

I think the first 3 and the last are reasonable interpretations given what the rules actually say.

As for realism, you are talking about having M1 rifle (with an 8 round clip) multiplied at x4 generating more FP than a crewed heavy machine gun even with no multipliers.  Clearly that doesn't make sense.

In the absence of actual errata and the fact that I have never seen this situation come up in actual play of 100's of games, I think the "each doubling results in increasing the FP multiplier by 1" is the best interpretation.

I just read the relevant rules:
Flanking doubles the firepower of the group that is flanking (rule 17.4)
Infiltration doubles the firepower of the individual that has infiltrated (rule 20.51)
A hero card doubles the firepower of an individual or triples it if it is already doubled. (rule 10.45)
This specific situation is not mentioned in the errata.

I see several possibilities.
1. Infiltration and Flanking double firepower for the same reason (fire coming from an advantageous direction). Because of this, they do not stack. (net x3 FP from the infiltrator).
2. Infiltration doubles individaual firepower, Hero increases individual FP to triple, group FP is then doubled (net x6 FP for the infiltrator).

I lean towards #1 - neither infiltration nor flanking say that they do anything when the firepower is already doubled.  They also both have the same exclusion (flamethrowers). To me, this tends to indicate that infiltration is merely individual flanking, and thus shouldn't be doubled again. Even if the infiltrator is firing from a different advantageous direction, he then isn't firing from the same direction as the flanking group, and shouldn't get the flanking bonus.

No it is NOT an interesting question, but an overly silly misreading of the rule.

ground_truth_answer:
If a Russian player takes these 3 actions 
Fire, Rally, Movement ...and he has a terrain card Stream in his hand May he play the terrain on his opponent?   

A) Fire, Movement, Rally are all actions.  A Russian player CANNOT discard any cards if they do any actions (With two exceptions:  Elite 
troops, Entrenchment)

B)  Playing ANY CARD on an opponent (terrain, wire, sniper) is ALWAYS done with a discard.

Because of A & B, the answer is no.

And refill his hand to 4 cards ? Or must he hold the stream in his hand and refill only 3 cards

Refilling your hand to 4 cards means to draw as many AS NECESSARY until you have 4 cards.  If you no cards in hand at the end of the turn, you draw 4.  If you have 1 card left in your hand, you draw 3.  2 cards left, draw 2.  3 cards left, draw 1.  Or 4 cards left  (If you only performed entrenchments, weapon repair, etc.), draw 0.
 

If a Russian player has 4 terrain cards in his hand 3 Marsh 1 Stream could he play all 4 onto the opponents [(4)groups with move cards ] and Refill his hand ?
OR
must he discard  the terrain into the discard pile and refill at the end of his turn?
ManyThanksToner

Since playing terrain on an opponent *****IS***** a discard.  So yes, you can play as many terrain cards on your opponent, so long as it legal to discard (i.e. no actions, except entrenchment.)

You ALWAYS refill your hand at the end of your turn, whether you played cards for actions or discarded.

query:
Campaign Game Promotions: After years of using the Campaign rules for Up Front, I noticed something which made me wonder whether I've been playing them wrong all this time.  This has to do with marking slashes in the "Promotion" column.

What I've been doing is putting a slash in the Promotion column every time a man increases his Morale or Panic value by accumulating 5 Elan points (42.44), and putting a slash in the "Survival" column each time he survives a scenario (42.45).  Then, a man increases his rank (eg from PFC to CPL) when he has 10 slashes in the Survival and Promotion columns combined (erasing those slashes).  So, for example, a CPL who has survived 6 scenarios and has increased his M3P4 to M5P6 (ie 4 increments) is promoted to SGT. Fine.  

However, I noticed for the first time that, in the notes at the bottom of the US and Russian rosters, it says for column 9 (Promotion): "Enter / if in play at game end; enter / whenever man improves rating".  This would mean that a man who survives a scenario always gets two slashes (one in Survival, one in Promotion) and may get a second in Promotion if he gains an M/P increment.  Thus, accumulating 10 slashes in the two columns taken together will obviously be much quicker - taking about half the number of scenarios.

So, I can see three possibilities:

1) Take this as read, such that any man who participates in and survives every scenario of a 10-game campaign is guaranteed two promotions even if he gains no M/P increments.

2) This is a misprint: when preparing the rosters, someone did a copy and paste and accidentally included the "Enter / if in play at game end;" phrase under the "Promotion" column when it should only have been against the "Survival" column.

3) This is an editing mistake: the original idea was to enter survival slashes only under "Survival" and aggregate the "Survival" and "Promotion" columns to determine promotion.  Then it occurred to someone that, if you noted survival in both columns, you need not add them together, so they put the note under the "Promotion" column - but they forgot to amend the rules in sections 42.44-45 to match.

Anyone got any comments or ideas?

ground_truth_answer:
Hi, just a quick question about encirclement. Does encirclement prevent the encircled group from retreating? 

No.  You may still retreat.  One way to break encirclement is get bother encircling groups in front of the encircled group, that is done by retreating at least twice.
 
[17.62]    An encircled group remains encircled until either opposing group which comprises the encirclement is eliminated, or infiltrated by the encircled group, or changes its group ID chit [17.7], or is at Relative Range 1 or less from the encircled group, or both encircling groups find themselves "in front of" the encircled group.

but...if you retreat, are you not retreating into the group that encircle you? 

Nope.  The "encircling" group is adjacent to (and does not have the same letter as) the opponent's group it is encircling.   Only groups with the same ID chit letter block each other.

query:
Infiltration + wire + capture: Lets say that my moving group in a forest succesfully inflitrates an enemy group positioned in a building.

On his turn my opponent plays wire on my group.

I CC him and kill all of his men.

I decide to capture his building.

According to rules when a moving group captures an opponent's terrain  the move card is discarted.

What about the wire? Does it stay or it also discarted?
title: Infiltration + wire + capture
raw_question:
Lets say that my moving group in a forest succesfully inflitrates an enemy group positioned in a building.

On his turn my opponent plays wire on my group.

I CC him and kill all of his men.

I decide to capture his building.

According to rules when a moving group captures an opponent's terrain  the move card is discarted.

What about the wire? Does it stay or it also discarted?
ground_truth_answer:
If you infiltrate and then are thrown in wire, you may attempt CC.  In that you are correct. 

But, you can't take the opposing terrain after eliminating the last man while infiltrating--You are in wire and the only terrain that can be placed while you are in wire is Open Ground, which goes underneath the wire..  

 13.34   Neither Terrain nor Movement cards can be placed on top of a Wire card by either player; the Wire card must first be removed by play of a temporary Movement card. Note that a group on Wire may not play a Movement card to remove the Wire as long as that group contains a pinned man.

13.5   Open Ground may be placed beneath a Wire or Smoke card and above a Movement card by the moving player so as to eliminate his group's Moving status, yet leave the Wire and/or Smoke in play.

The rule makes no distinction between playing of a card (from either hand) or terrain capture.  I see no reason why that would make a difference.

Terrain Capture rules make clear that its use is completely optional:

20.8 TERRAIN CAPTURE:   
    Whenever the last man in a group is eliminated while his group is infiltrated, the Terrain card his group occupied (including entrenchments) is subject to capture by any group currently infiltrating that group regardless of the movement status of either group. The captor has the choice of replacing his own Terrain card with that of the eliminated defender's, or simply removing the eliminated group's cards to the Discard pile. Note that if two different groups can claim capture of the defender's Terrain card, it cannot be given to both groups, but that player can choose which of his groups to give it to. He could also transfer any man currently infiltrating that group during that turn into the group which receives the captured Terrain card. Any Movement cards in play on either the captor or the eliminated group are removed when the Terrain card is placed on its new group.

The mandatory rule 13.34 has precedence over rule 20.8 which merely gives you the opportunity to capture opposing terrain--subject to other rules.

Hi all, we are trying to learn how to play this incredible game, but there are some rules which we are not sure if we understand. In particular, in order to play a Flank card, it has to be played sideways. What does this mean exactly?

a) Does this mean that the group is doing a side movement? In this case, can the group receive a terrain card? Do they suffer the +1 attack strength modifier?

b) Are the soldiers of the group moving, i.e., bolt rifles multiply by 0.5 their FP, MMG cannot fire, attack strength is divided by 2 and so on.

c) Can you use a FLANK movement card to ford a stream? And to exit a marsh?

Thanks!

David

In general, a Flank Movement card does everything a normal Movement card does, including when played sideways to obtain Flanking.  So yes, all the above effects occur: the group is moving sideways and can receive a Terrain card (either from its owner or by enemy discard), incoming Fire attacks are +1, and they suffer the Moving Fire disadvantages.  However, the group is Flanking while the Movement card is in play, so Bolt-Action rifles are halved and doubled (ie retain their normal FP).  Semi-auto rifles double their FP like other weapons.  Fire Strength is still halved and rounded down.

It can also be used to Ford or while in a Marsh, with some special but logical effects:
- if you use it to Ford, and fail (red RNC), the Movement card goes away and you don't get the Flanking advantage.
- if you use it for the first Marsh exit card, you can't play a Terrain card until you've played a second Movement card - which removes the Flanking, unless the second card is also a Flank card and is played sideways.

The group retains Flanking when it plays or receives a Terrain card, so you can Flank, then play a Hill for maximum effect.  You lose the Flank by moving or receiving a Wire card, or if the Flanked group plays a Movement card (even to remove Wire - so think hard before discarding Wire on a Flanked group).

One thing often forgotten is that, in order to Flank, the Flanking group has to be adjacent but not opposite to the Flanked group, and there has to be a friendly group opposite to the Flanked group.  So if you have groups A, B, C and the enemy has groups A & B, your A can Flank his B, your B can flank his A, your C can Flank his B; his A can Flank your B, his B can Flank your A; but his B can't Flank your C because he has no group opposite your C.

And finally, you can't combine Flanking with Lateral Group Transfer (eg moving group B to group C) because of the above rule that an opposite group must exist before you Flank.  This again is logical if you think about it.

There are some other details about Natural Flanking and (Heaven help us) Encircled, but read section 17 carefully and it should come clear.

Good luck!

B(2)     B(0)     B(10)

Please enlighten me!

R.:)
ground_truth_answer:
Surrounded is a very confusing set up the way it is described in the rule book.  Bruce Wigdor's IUF program implements it is the surrounding player sets groups at both RC0 and RC10, the defender is its RC0.  For game purposes, the groups at RC10 are designated Group I, J, K, etc.

The attacking groups at RC0 advance towards the defender normally, by increasing their RC number.  The attacking groups at RC10 advance towards the defender by LOWERING their RC number.

The defender advances towards the RC0 groups by increasing their RC into the positive numbers, and towards the RC10 groups by DECREASING  (-2 < -1) their RC into the negative numbers.

The standard relative range rules including the correction for RR over 5 (if sum of RC > 5 then RR = 10 - (sum of RC's)) always work out in this system:

Attacker at RC 2 fires at defender at RC 1 => RR = 2+1 = 3
Attacker at RC 2 fires at defender at RC-1 => RR = 2-1 = 1
Attacker at RC 8 fires at defender at RC 1 => RR = 8+1 = 9 converts to 10-9 = 1
Attacker at RC 8 fires at defender at RC-1 => RR = 8-1 = 7 converts to 10-7 = 3

(All of these assume firing is at groups with same ID letter or one letter off (i,e, directly opposite or adjacent opposite groups)

If everything is laid out on a board:

Att RC   Def RC    
0          5       Attacker starts here
1          4
2          3
3          2
4          1
5          0       Defender starts here
6         -1
7         -2
8         -3
9         -4
10        -5        Attacker starts here
 

Now onto encirclement:

Essentially, Encirclement has to be done from groups that start on the SAME side but otherwise happens per normal rules:  

An encircling group B that started at RR0 must reach "RR6" (i.e. RR4 behind the defender group A they are encircling) and then play the sideways movement card (while also having their own group A) to create the encirclement.  (This is the normal encirclement rule) 

An encircling group J that started at RR10 must reach RR4 (thus passing the defending group A they are encircling) and then play a sideways movement card (while having their own group I) to create the encirclement.

Groups that started on opposite sides cannot combine for an encirclement.   

So:  Attacker group B may encircle Defending group A below:
AF1:  A(0)  B(6)
DF:   A(0)  B(-2)
AF2:  I(0)  J(0)

Likewise Attacker group J may encircle Defending group A below:
AF1:  A(0)  B(0)
DF:   A(0)  B(2)
AF2:  I(0)  J(4)

It actually works out reasonably well after a game or two on IUF.  

And it is an interesting scenario of both sides.  
-  The attacker can't put too much strength in one of the two sides, the defender will move towards the smaller/safer force.  He can't lose too much in one force, because the defender will crush that side and run.
-  If the defender can't weaken one of the sides and advance towards it, he is usually picked apart.

Actually X is a pretty balanced scenario--except Japanese defense (75% break is the killer.)  One of my favorites and worth the effort.

query:
Infiltration question: This came up in a wargameroom league game, and we couldn't find an answer.

We are playing Scenario F. He has group A/B/C with group A moving to RC4.

My Group B is moving at RC1. I successfully infiltrate his group with 1 guy. This stops the RC4 victory condition for that group (for now).

He discards a Minefield onto my Group B. I reject the terrain moving back to RC0.

The question is do I lose the infiltrator in my Group B? If so, what is the appropriate rules reference (20.53 does not seem to indicate I do)?
title: Infiltration question
raw_question:
This came up in a wargameroom league game, and we couldn't find an answer.

We are playing Scenario F. He has group A/B/C with group A moving to RC4.

My Group B is moving at RC1. I successfully infiltrate his group with 1 guy. This stops the RC4 victory condition for that group (for now).

He discards a Minefield onto my Group B. I reject the terrain moving back to RC0.

The question is do I lose the infiltrator in my Group B? If so, what is the appropriate rules reference (20.53 does not seem to indicate I do)?
ground_truth_answer:
I guess that must simulate known minefilds or something.
Bingo.

Rule 52.11 says "a player can always reject a Minefield card discarded upon him (7.3), but if he accepts it the Minefield may be in fact real or a fake. The accepting player must immediately draw a RNC to determine if the minefield is real. If he draws a black RNC=>1 the minefield is real. If he draws a 0 or red RNC, the minefield is a fake and is immediately flipped to the Open Ground side."

What I was trying to do was keep my infiltrator in B protected by having him at RC0 and RR4 to the infiltrated group A. Since my group A after the rejected terrain was at RC1, he would have to either attack and pin the infiltrator in my group B or try to eliminate my group A, move up, to infiltrate and enter close combat. Either is much more difficult than just simply accepting the terrain (since good odds of it being a fake) and having him infiltrate and close combat the 3 guys in the group.

I reject the terrain, He drops his in some defensive terrain for the win. Hopefully this will be fixed in future iterations of the program.

Ordnance and Flanking Fire. Any opinions?: When it comes to Flanking Fire, the rules clearly state that the Firepower of the flanking group is doubled. From this I take it that ordnance receive no bonus whatsoever for being in a flanking position. Is this correct or am I missing something? Shouldn't ordnance also benefit in some way for flanking a group? As with most other aspects of this game, I guess there is a logic also behind this. It might even be a striking logic. I think I've just failed to see it so far.

Would it be too much to give ordnance in a flanking position a, say, +1 to the To Hit frequency? So far I've played this "by the book", but I've many times been tempted to introduce this as a house-rule. Is the logic maybe that this makes ordnance too powerful? Although I won't say that boosting a mortar's TH with one is, relatively, more powerful than boosting a group's FP from 9 to 18.

Any opinions on the subject from you other wondeful grognards of this wonderful game?

R.:)

ground_truth_answer:
Well, the mortar round is coming almost staright down, so it doesn't matter as much which direction it's coming from so I don't think mortars deserve a flanking bonus.

Whiile I could see an argument for direct fire ordnance getting the bonus I don't think it does, under the rules, and I think you can argue it the other way just as easily.

I think the idea behind flanking fire is the psychological as well as physical effect of bullets coming in from all sides. There's no place to hide. The to-hit process used for ordnance implies less volume of fire, so the effect of bullets flying in from different directions is reduced.

Opposing group is moving Forward.

If I am playing a nationality that can discard 2 cards, can I discard 1 terrain onto the group to see if they accept or reject and then discard the 2nd terrain on the same group?

title: Discard Question

Opposing group is moving Forward.

If I am playing a nationality that can discard 2 cards, can I discard 1 terrain onto the group to see if they accept or reject and then discard the 2nd terrain on the same group?

(Obviously you could only do this if they rejected the first terrain and change their movement to from forward to sideways.)

Thanks in advance as I don't have the rules in front of me.
ground_truth_answer:
From the Errata site:

4.3 & 14.5 During a multi-card discard, can the player observe the results of one discard before deciding where and/or if to discard another?
A. No. Rule 7.3 and 7.32 specifically state that discards are resolved prior to the next turn, not prior to the next discard.

Discard Capability, 4.32, 4.33, 14.5 and 44.1 Can nationalities with multi-card discard capability discard two or more wires on a single group in a single turn?
A. Yes.

Examples:
[NOTE: The examples assume that the indicated discards are valid for the scenario and situation (i.e. the discarding side has sniper capability).]

Non-moving Group: May discard any number of SNIPERS and/or any number of WIRE cards.

Moving Group: May discard one terrain card and/or any number of snipers and/or any number of WIRE cards. Rejecting the terrain does NOT reject the WIRE. If the terrain is accepted and WIRE is not allowed in that type of terrain (e.g. MARSH) then the WIRE is discarded.

Two Moving Groups Exchanging Group Letters: Same as a moving group with two additions. If either group rejects a terrain discard, the position exchange is cancelled. If terrain is discarded on one group and accepted, the moving player MUST complete the position exchange by placing the other group in terrain (including open ground) on his next turn.

query:
Up Front  MUD rules: There have been several suggestions for representing muddy conditions in Up Front (AHG 22/3, 28/4), requiring a group to play a Movement card in sideways mode before playing another Movement card (in a later turn) to move forwards or back.  There are a couple of consequences of this which may or may not be intended:

1) The opponent can prevent movement by discarding terrain on this initial Movement card.

2) Any move which changes range renders the moving group liable to the +2 to incoming fire.

Does anyone have a view on whether either or both of these are deliberate? - as together they make movement very difficult, perhaps more so than is workable.  My feeling is that the intention was simply to require the play of two Movement cards to change range, which effectively halves the number of forward moves a side can make during a game.

One could fairly easily obviate either or both of the two effects I mention above:

1) Disallow terrain discard on the preliminary Movement card (although this would prevent a "legitimate" discard on a true sideways move).

2) Remove the first Movement card when the second (forward or backward) card is played. 

However, it's questionable whether the effects were in fact intended - what do you think?

ground_truth_answer:
Unless you're representing a real quicksand-like morass, I think this makes things go too far.
Actual movement under combat conditions isn't very fast anyway, in a larger sense, and I think the normal movement rules already depict that. Muddy ground may make it harder to dash between points of cover, but a better way to handle that might be to allow cower cards to be played with some kind of effect that hinders movement.

I tend to agree, which is why I raised the question in the first place.  I suspect the author of the variant didn't bottom out the effects.  In experimenting with this, we have raised some questions about what happens when terrain is rejected - do you have to play yet another sideways card to get started again?  All in all I'm not convinced it's properly thought out.

But I wanted to get the views of other Up Front players ...

Another effect of muddy ground is to reduce the effect of high explosive.

Yes - the variant rules allow a -1 to Fire Strength of HE attacks.  I don't think there's any problem with that.

BTW, I still occasionally re-read your article about historicity of wargames in the AHG!

query:
Rule Questions: Close Combat pairings, Retrogade back into terrain, Panzerfaust fired on the move: I'm very satisfied with the Up Front rules since they are so incredibly tight that I never had any rule unclarity for more than 20 plays. However my last play brought up the following questions (one rule unclarity and two general concerns):

1) Close Combat pairings

When for example two attacker engage three (unpinned) defenders in close combat and each of the attackers assaults one of the defenders, what does the third defender do?

Rule 20.622 addresses this for attackers, but in regard to defenders it refers to rule 20.71, which is limited to multi-man crews. Moreover, it is not explained which CC pairing the unengaged defenders would support. Is the third defender in the example above simply left out of the close combats?

I also have these concerns with the rules, which I'd like to hear your opinion on:

2) Shouldn't a group which moved out of terrain, but then reverses its movement be allowed to reenter the terrain they left?

3) Rule 25.32 states that only (certain) AFVs may fire while moving. It is clear to me that you can't fire an Anti-Tank rifle or a mortar while moving, but shouldn't it be possible to fire a Panzerfaust (which doesn't have recoil) on the move, applying rules 25.32 and 25.33? By the way rule 30.1 clearly forbids firing a Panzerfaust while moving.
title: Rule Questions: Close Combat pairings, Retrogade back into terrain, Panzerfaust fired on the move
raw_question:
I'm very satisfied with the Up Front rules since they are so incredibly tight that I never had any rule unclarity for more than 20 plays. However my last play brought up the following questions (one rule unclarity and two general concerns):

1) Close Combat pairings

When for example two attacker engage three (unpinned) defenders in close combat and each of the attackers assaults one of the defenders, what does the third defender do?

Rule 20.622 addresses this for attackers, but in regard to defenders it refers to rule 20.71, which is limited to multi-man crews. Moreover, it is not explained which CC pairing the unengaged defenders would support. Is the third defender in the example above simply left out of the close combats?

I also have these concerns with the rules, which I'd like to hear your opinion on:

2) Shouldn't a group which moved out of terrain, but then reverses its movement be allowed to reenter the terrain they left?

3) Rule 25.32 states that only (certain) AFVs may fire while moving. It is clear to me that you can't fire an Anti-Tank rifle or a mortar while moving, but shouldn't it be possible to fire a Panzerfaust (which doesn't have recoil) on the move, applying rules 25.32 and 25.33? By the way rule 30.1 clearly forbids firing a Panzerfaust while moving.
ground_truth_answer:
1) Close Combat pairings

When for example two attacker engage three (unpinned) defenders in close combat and each of the attackers assaults one of the defenders, what does the third defender do?

Nothing, he is just watching (or distracted or unaware of the ongoing fight).

Is the third defender in the example above simply left out of the close combats?

This is correct.

As per 20.52 CC ENTRY, the attacking player draws one RPC for each of his men who is capable of entering Close Combat (i.e. each man must have Infiltrator status AND each man must either pass a Morale Check or you play a Movement Card to the discard pile for him instead.) The RPC then determines the target of the CC.

Since target selection happens randomly, you can end up with both attackers in your example attacking the same man while the other two men in the infiltrated group aren't attacked. Thus they don't take part in the CC at all.

Remember: if more than one man is attacking the same target in CC, you don't add their Close Combat Values (CCV) but add a +3 modifier to the primary attacker's CCV (which preferably should be the Personality Card with the highest CCV).

2) Shouldn't a group which moved out of terrain, but then reverses its movement be allowed to reenter the terrain they left?

No. To do this, you will have to play two Movement Cards, one in forward mode, the second in reverse mode. As per 5.2, the second movement card played will remove the terrain card. This means that you end up in Open Ground with two active movement cards, yielding your opponent a +2 modifier for his fire attacks (ugh!).

3) Rule 25.32 states that only (certain) AFVs may fire while moving. It is clear to me that you can't fire an Anti-Tank rifle or a mortar while moving, but shouldn't it be possible to fire a Panzerfaust (which doesn't have recoil) on the move, applying rules 25.32 and 25.33? By the way rule 30.1 clearly forbids firing a Panzerfaust while moving.

As you are stating correctly, rule 30.1 forbids Panzerfaust being fired on the move. Rule 25.32 and 25.33 deal with Ordnance weapons of AFVs. Ordnance only may fire while on the move as an AFVs primary weapon. As a corollary, you must not fire Infantry Guns on the move.

I'm very satisfied with the Up Front rules since they are so incredibly tight that I never had any rule unclarity for more than 20 plays.

I'm glad that you see it like this. There's a lot of ranting going on here on the 'Geek about the rules, but I'm with you on this one. To me the rules of Up Front are very concise and in my games I have never encountered a situation which couldn't be resolved using the rules.

Enjoy your games, don't hurry too much, but get common with the newly learned rules first instead before moving on to new things. And when you are REALLY familiar with the rule set, try "Up Front 501 City Fight in four" with design-your-own squads. Simply fantastic!

Dudes,
This is truly the greatest man to man game ever made. My brother and I have played this game since the mid 1980s and play it every single time we get together...usually at holidays. Honest, you will. Have fun with your new game...mine is quite far from new. But it has seen a thousand skirmishes and a million flamethrower malfunctions...damned flamethrowers.
Peace out.
DWR

query:
Rule 19: What's the difference between a weapon with FP0 and one with "no firepower at the current range"?: At the end of the thread concerning lateral group transfer from Marsh, Dan (voynix) and I ended up discussing certain aspects with rule 19 governing malfunctions. There seem to be some contradictions within that rule. And to top it up, I've found two different clarifications to the rule. More on that later.

The contradicting points are these (I quote from the rule):

1. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a firing weapon, that weapon malfunctions and combat vs any remaining defenders not yet fired upon is resolved with one less Fire Strength for every two Firepower factors (or fraction thereof) previously contributed by the malfunctioned weapon.

2. If the RPC indicates a position occupied by a designated assistant crewman of a firing MG or a man whose weapon has no firepower at its current range, the malfunction is considered only momentary, and the fire against any remaining defenders in the defending group yet to be attacked is resolved with one less Fire Strength, but no weapon malfunctions.

As I understand the rule, a weapon with FP0 on the current range is also a firing weapon. And consequently it will malfunction and the rest of the attack will be resolved with one less fire strength, -if we consider 0 to be a fraction of two firepower factors (I do).

But what then constitutes a weapon, as of my point 2, that has no firepower factors at its current range? It can't be ordnance  because those weapons are clearly defined as being non-firing during normal fire-attacks. And flamethrowers can be used only on RR5 and then at the owning player's will.

To make matters worse, I have two different clarifications from what seems to be two versions of Andrew Maly's official errata. The clarifcation I have an outprint of (I don't remeber from where I printed it out) states:

Weapon with 0 Firepower at the current range - no malfunction, continue attack with -1FS.

While the clarification on the Up Front Main Page states:

Weapon with 0 Firepower at the current range - weapon malfunctions, continue attack with -0 FS.

???????

Which one is correct, if any?

Personally I play like this:

Weapon with 0 Firepower at the current range - weapon malfunctions, continue attack with -1FS.

The best (worst) of both worlds as I see it. And, frankly, I'm going to continue to play like that because I think that is what makes most sense. If a firing weapon malfunctions, you should get a penalty even if it has FP0. In a real-life situation, the volume of fire would decrease with any firing weapon malfunctioning, even if the accuracy of the fire isn't getting any worse. After all. What pins a man is the impression of the volume of fire - how much lead is flying around his ears, even if the lead on RR0 is less likely to do any physical damage. And in the case of the MG-crewman, a -1FS can easily be considered a slight, temporary setup in the handling of the MG instead of the crewman's weapon malfunctioning. So I totally agree with that one.

But anyway I'd like some comments on this problem. Andrew? Richard? Anyone?

R.:)

ground_truth_answer:
No firepower at the current range is indicative of, but not limited to, Flamethrowers at Relative Range 0-4 and Ordnance Weapons.

I was thinking along the same lines, but then Ordnance and Flamethrowers are, in the paranthesis of rule 19.13, specified as being non-firing. And if the RPC indicates a position occupied by a non-firing weapon, there is no effect. What is then the difference between a non-firing weapon and a weapon with no Firepower factors at its current range for the sake of malfunction?

Check UF official errata on Andy's website--it contains a complete rewrite to handle all of the issues with 19.11 and 19.13.  This rule caused a lot of discussion on UF mailing lists at the time--mainly because all of the contradictions between these two rules:  
-  how to handle different malf numbers (i.e. 5), 
-  when a weapon is the "sole firing weapon" referred to in 19.11 vs. 19.13 which calls for an RPC draw including 0FP and non-firing men, etc.
-  Exactly which men are considered "non-firing" have "0FP at current range"

19 Weapon Malfunction

If an Ordnance weapon is firing using the To Hit process (25.3), and the To Hit RNC is in the range of the malfunction values for that weapon, the Ordnance weapon malfunctions, automatically.

If a group is conducting a Fire Attack (6) then ALL weapons in the group are considered to be firing with the following exceptions:

    * Flamethrowers designated as not firing
    * Secondary weapons (e.g. Demo Charge, panzerfaust)
    * Ordnance
    * Non-firing infiltrators
    * Weapons of designated assistant crewmen (however, continue reading)

If an RNC drawn to resolve the Fire Attack is equal to the malfunction value of only one weapon, that weapon malfunctions automatically, and no RPC is drawn to determine which weapon malfunctions.

Example: Japanese Group comprised of R, R, R, LMG. The RNC is a RED 5. The LMG automatically malfunctions, because it is the only weapon with a malfunction value of a RED 5.

If the group is comprised of only one armed man, that weapon automatically malfunctions, and no RPC is drawn.

Example: In the following four groups: (R; MP; LMG; R, Unarmed Man), no RPC is drawn to determine which weapon malfunctions.

If none of the previous cases applies, then an RPC is drawn to determine which position is affected by the malfunction. Do include Unarmed men, and DO NOT include Men transferring. The following results and their impacts are (use the first case that applies):

    * Unarmed man - no effect.
    * Man is currently pinned - weapon malfunctions, no effect on FS.
    * Ordnance weapon or its designated crewman - no effect. Note that an ATR using FP is not considered firing as ordnance, and therefore both the ATR and the crewman are subject to malfunction.
    * Designated non-firing Flamethrower or Infiltrator - no effect
    * Designated crewman of a firing MG - no malfunction, contine attack with -1 FS
    * Weapon with 0 Firepower at the current range - weapon malfunctions, continue attack with -0 FS
    * Firing weapon malfunctions, and attack continues with one less FS for every 2 FP factors the weapon was contributing to the attack, fractions rounded up.

Malfunctioned weapons have a base malfunction number of red 6 regardless of the malfunction number printed on the card.

query:
Lateral Transfer From a Marsh: The 17.7 rules clearly state that a lateral transfer is not complete until a new Terrain Card is placed upon the sideways Movement card used to initiate the lateral transfer.   Regarding a Marsh, the rules state:

A group in a Marsh may change identity by playing one Movement card, but still requires two Movement cards to exit that marsh

How can that group in the Marsh change its identity chit by playing one Movement card, since the above rules state that a new Terrain card must be played to complete the lateral transfer?

Thanks in advance
title: Lateral Transfer From a Marsh
raw_question:
The 17.7 rules clearly state that a lateral transfer is not complete until a new Terrain Card is placed upon the sideways Movement card used to initiate the lateral transfer.   Regarding a Marsh, the rules state:

A group in a Marsh may change identity by playing one Movement card, but still requires two Movement cards to exit that marsh

How can that group in the Marsh change its identity chit by playing one Movement card, since the above rules state that a new Terrain card must be played to complete the lateral transfer?

Thanks in advance
ground_truth_answer:
Richard, I think you are wrong.

Roar,  Every tournament has interpreted this way including WBC.  That how it is interpreted by Bruce Wigdor's Internet Up Front Program.

 Because rule 17. 7 clearly states that "A group in a Marsh may change identity by playing only one Movement card, but still requires two movement cards to exit the Marsh".

You are ignoring 8.42.  I won't repeat it again.

I can't see that this can possibly be interpreted in any other way than that the Marsh makes an exeption to the rule regarding that you have to play a terrain card to complete the group ID change. Otherwise I think it would be just too difficult to make a lateral group transfer from the Marsh.

Under the correct interpretation, a lateral transfer is just as difficult as  any other movement out of Marsh.

Why do you think it should be EASIER to laterally transfer as opposed to say advancing/retreating/changing terrain in the same position?  

The second Movement card played on a March allows you to do anything you can normally do from other terrain (except Stream) with a movement card

Yes, and that fact also tells me that the first movement card played to exit a marsh in addition can be regarded as the terrain card you end up in after having made a lateral group transfer. The parenthesis you mention in rule 8.42 I believe only serves to clarify the fact that it is the second movement card that indicates wether you change your 
range chit or not.  

Two reasons your interpretation is wrong

- You are adding words that are not there:  "Lateral" applies to ALL lateral moves, whether they are group transfers or not.  They are CALLED "Lateral Group Transfers" after all.
- Lateral movements DO NOT change the range chit.  So your purported reason for the rules must be wrong.

Anyway. Rule 17.7 is the rule covering the topic of lateral group transfer and thus should take presedence over any other rule that appears to contradict it. 

The rule is badly written, but if you interpret it that way you do, you break 8.42.  The correct way does not break the 8.42.

I'll play it this way until Don Greenwood comes out and tells me otherwise!

I happen to know Don Greenwood (as do most other WBCers).  He would tell you bring it up with Andy Maly, the Up Front Errata Keeper for many years.

Here Andy's Website:
http://home.comcast.net/~upfront2000/

Here is his 'GEEK page:
http://www.boardgamegeek.com/user/upfront2000

Even better you can join Andy & I and many other gamers at the WBC!

query:
Retrograde movement and range chits: Rule 5.62 suggests that players readjust range chits that are > 5 or < 0 after a deck shuffle.  In the rulebook example, Black group A is at range 6 and Red group A is at range -2.  After readjustment, Black is at range 4 and Red is at range 0.  

My question is: isn't this a potential disadvantage for Black?  Previously, if Red advanced to RR 5, it would still be at range -1 and therefore unable to retreat without a red RNC move card (5.51).  After readjustment, Red can advance to RR 5 and later retreat using any move card.  

Since Red has more tactical options as a result of readjustment, isn't it in Black's interest to decline readjustment?  Or am I reading the rules wrong?
title: Retrograde movement and range chits
raw_question:
Rule 5.62 suggests that players readjust range chits that are > 5 or < 0 after a deck shuffle.  In the rulebook example, Black group A is at range 6 and Red group A is at range -2.  After readjustment, Black is at range 4 and Red is at range 0.  

My question is: isn't this a potential disadvantage for Black?  Previously, if Red advanced to RR 5, it would still be at range -1 and therefore unable to retreat without a red RNC move card (5.51).  After readjustment, Red can advance to RR 5 and later retreat using any move card.  

Since Red has more tactical options as a result of readjustment, isn't it in Black's interest to decline readjustment?  Or am I reading the rules wrong?
ground_truth_answer:
I think you read the rules right. As I too see it, this readjustment would benefit the red group. When I play, we never readjust the way described.

One of the special rules from Deer Valleys campaign rules actually demand, when in use, that the players readjust after each deck so that the most withdrawn group is advanced to range 0 and all the other groups are adjusted accordingly to maintain Relative Range. This rule is mostly used with scenarios where the attacker wins by reaching a certain range chit. Or the first player to reach a certain range chit will win and the attacker will loose if noone reaches the required range chit. And the sole purpose of this special rule is to discomfort the defined attacker by putting pressure on him to reach the required range chit as soon as possible.

So, yes, the example in the rulebook will, most times, be a detriment to the attacking side, -obviously the black group in your example.

R.:)

query:
2 more rules questions...: 1. Opponent has Group B at Range Chit 3 and in a Gully. I have Group D at Range Chit 3. Can my Group D fire into the Gully? They are at RR5, but doesn't seem right to fire over a group into a gully.
2. Can I do an individual transfer into a group that is moving at the same range chit? We couldn't find anything in the rules forbidding it. I just want to make sure.
title: 2 more rules questions...
raw_question:
1. Opponent has Group B at Range Chit 3 and in a Gully. I have Group D at Range Chit 3. Can my Group D fire into the Gully? They are at RR5, but doesn't seem right to fire over a group into a gully.
2. Can I do an individual transfer into a group that is moving at the same range chit? We couldn't find anything in the rules forbidding it. I just want to make sure.
ground_truth_answer:
1. Opponent has Group B at Range Chit 3 and in a Gully. I have Group D at Range Chit 3. Can my Group D fire into the Gully? They are at RR5, but doesn't seem right to fire over a group into a gully.

They are at RR3, not RR5.  If the two groups were adjacent (eg groups B and C), they would be at RR4, as they have moved "past" each other.  Since they are non-adjacent, they are one range further away - hence RR3.  So they can't fire at each other - unless your Group D is on a Hill.

If you find this confusing, draw up a 4x6 grid and put the groups in the appropriate boxes - it will make more sense.

2. Can I do an individual transfer into a group that is moving at the same range chit? We couldn't find anything in the rules forbidding it. I just want to make sure.

Yes, you can.  The rule [17.8] says: "An unpinned man in a group which is neither encircled, nor on Wire/Minefield, may transfer from one group to an adjacent friendly group with the same range chit by placing a Movement card in the discard tray for each man he wishes to transfer as the sole action of the sending group for that turn...."  There is no stipulation about the movement status of either group at the start of the transfer.  There is a prohibition that neither group may change its range chit until the transfer is complete.

query:
Stream fire strength: From 8.52:

A medium machine gun, mortar, or Infantry Gun may not fire from a Stream, although an AFV's weapons may fire from a Stream with no detriment at all. Other crewed weapons may fire from a Stream only if they are fully crewed and non-moving, and even then must use their bracketed Firepower or To Hit frequency. The Fire Strength of any other group attacking from a Stream using non-ordnance weapons is reduced by one. A panzerfaust fired from a Stream must reduce its To Hit frequency by one.
Emphasis mine.  A non-moving German group in a Stream is attacking with a Fire 3/6 card.  The group consists of fully crewed LMG plus 3 rifles (1 rifle is serving as crew).  Does the presence of the fully crewed LMG exempt it from the "any other group" clause, and thus fire at Fire Strength 3?

ground_truth_answer:
Scott is correct:

To individual transfer (in rules parlance)
-  The groups must be adjacent, at the same range chit, and there must be an unpinned SL or ASL in either group.
-  Sending group cannot be in wire or minefield, or a Marsh unless there is a sideways (enforced delay) movement card on it.  If in an unforded stream, each transferring man needs a Ford movement card or passes a Ford (Black RNC = good) check.
-  A movement card must be played for each transferring man.  Any number of men in a group can start a transfer on a single turn so long as a movement card is played for each man.
-  On a later turn, the accepting group can use its action to take in all of the men transferring to it from one group.
-  Until a transfering man is accepted by his destination group, he can be fired on when either the leaving or accepting group is fired upon  (Transferring should be first men resolved in a fire attack)  They get a +2 Defensive modifier.  And if pinned (unless a Hero is immediately played), he returns to his original group and is no longer transferring.

query:
A Question Regarding Snipers: When you play a sniper as a discard on a group you pull a card to see if that sniper kills or pins whomever he is shooting at. On the next turn - if the player chooses to - as the sole action of the group being sniped at - you can try to kill the sniper. Assuming that the sniper lives, we determined that he stays there and continues to shoot at that group until they are able to locate and kill him. We also determined that this shot takes place at the end of your turn, after you have performed an action (if possible/desired) on all of your groups and before discard(s). Is this correct? Or have we mangles the sniper rules?

Also - there is a limit of one sniper specified in the first scenario. I do not see this restriction in later scenarios but I do see a reference in the Do It Yourself scenario section that says you can opt for two snipers (don't recall specific language). Is there a limit to the number of snipers playable by each player in a scenario?

Thanks.
title: A Question Regarding Snipers
raw_question:
When you play a sniper as a discard on a group you pull a card to see if that sniper kills or pins whomever he is shooting at. On the next turn - if the player chooses to - as the sole action of the group being sniped at - you can try to kill the sniper. Assuming that the sniper lives, we determined that he stays there and continues to shoot at that group until they are able to locate and kill him. We also determined that this shot takes place at the end of your turn, after you have performed an action (if possible/desired) on all of your groups and before discard(s). Is this correct? Or have we mangles the sniper rules?

Also - there is a limit of one sniper specified in the first scenario. I do not see this restriction in later scenarios but I do see a reference in the Do It Yourself scenario section that says you can opt for two snipers (don't recall specific language). Is there a limit to the number of snipers playable by each player in a scenario?

Thanks.
ground_truth_answer:
My reading of 14.4 is that if the group is attacked twice and at least one armed man survives that group can use its action to make one sniper check and if successful that will count as one successful sniper check. You would use the lower of the two sniper result numbers to determine success of the check.

I think 14.4 would say in a two sniper attack you would:

1) specify which group or groups are being attacked by which sniper.

2) draw RPC for the position of the first sniper's victim.

3) draw the RNC for the success of the first sniper's attack.

4) if step 3 eliminated the last target in that group the discarding player can retarget the second sniper to a different group.

5) draw RPC for the second sniper.

6) draw RNC for the result of the second sniper. 

Then it will be the other player's turn and each group that was attacked and still has an armed, unpinned man can make a sniper check using the RNC of the sniper attack on that group. If both snipers attacked the same group that group gets only one check at the lower of the two RNC numbers.

query:
Noob questions (after first play): First of all--this is an amazing game. I have been a big fan of Combat Commander since its release, but I think Up Front is going to take its place in my traveling game box.

With that said, I am still trying to get all the rules under my belt. Here are a few that came up today that I couldnt find in the rulebook right away.

1. Scenario 1 has the first 5 buildings removed from RPC/RNC draws. When the deck is reshuffled, do these 5 buildings get shuffled back in?
2. One part of the victory condition for Scenario was to have 1 group at Range Chit 4. I just want to clarify it means Range Chit 4 and not Relative Range 4.
3. How many movement cards can you play on top of each other? The situation was this: 1 group on hill with Movement turned sideways. A 2nd Movement card is played on top that (enabling flanking fire). Then a 3rd movement played sideways (to encircle).
4. Is there anyway to play Up Front online?

Thanks in advance!
title: Noob questions (after first play)
raw_question:
First of all--this is an amazing game. I have been a big fan of Combat Commander since its release, but I think Up Front is going to take its place in my traveling game box.

With that said, I am still trying to get all the rules under my belt. Here are a few that came up today that I couldnt find in the rulebook right away.

1. Scenario 1 has the first 5 buildings removed from RPC/RNC draws. When the deck is reshuffled, do these 5 buildings get shuffled back in?
2. One part of the victory condition for Scenario was to have 1 group at Range Chit 4. I just want to clarify it means Range Chit 4 and not Relative Range 4.
3. How many movement cards can you play on top of each other? The situation was this: 1 group on hill with Movement turned sideways. A 2nd Movement card is played on top that (enabling flanking fire). Then a 3rd movement played sideways (to encircle).
4. Is there anyway to play Up Front online?

Thanks in advance!
ground_truth_answer:
No, it's+3. If your guys are moving, they're vulnerable to fire -- it doesn't matter which direction they're moving or what they're doing.

An attack can never be modified by +3 due to Movement. The maximum modifier  due to Movement would be +2. Rule 7.2 states:

The Fire Strength modifier of the last Terrain or Movement card placed upon a defending group is used when resolving any fire attacks against that group. If the last Terrain or Movement card played on a defending group is a Movement card, then the last played Terrain or Movement card placed prior to it in that group is also used (as well as any modifiers for Smoke/Wire cards above it).

So, even with three Movement cards in play on a group, the modifier for moving remains at +2. If the moving group is placed in Wire or attacked from a Hill, the modifier will be greater, but not due to the third (or more) Movement cards.

You're right ... now that I think about it, we usually pick up that first card if the third is ever played.

I probably have a couple guys in the boneyard that would have been saved by a better understanding of this rule.

ground_truth_answer:
1. Quick question on wounds.. if the primary crew operator is wounded, you could exchange weapons with the crew member.. would you then need to do a second action to switch the crew operator with the crew member after the weapon is exchanged?
Yes: one (automatic) action to acquire and then another action on a subsequent turn to assign a new crewman.

2. If a man is wounded, does he remain pinned?
A man wounded remains in the state he was at the time of the wound- unpinned or pinned. In other words, a wound result does not pin a man.

3. Wounded men give a victory point to your opponent if they survive to the end of the game, just as if he had routed?
Yes. In 16.42: "One Victory Point is awarded for each opposing wounded man or Rout removal." The 'or' appears to imply that if a wounded man routs, he is still worth only one Victory Point.

4. Flanking is removed if a terrain card is played on flanked group by either player, correct?
Yes. Don't flank when your opponent is moving.

5 a. How would the flanking group go about reflanking?
b. If a wire was put on the flanking group, and the wire is removed, does he get flanking back?
c. If the flanked group moves forward, is it possible to get into a position to reflank?
d. If the flanked group moves backward, would the flanking group just need to move forward one more time to flank again?
a. In all cases, the enemy group (such as Group B) must be opposed by an friendly group of the same Group ID (a Group B). Flanking occurs when an 'adjacent' friendly group (in this example, Group A or Group C) plays a Movement card to advance 'past' the enemy group to be flanked (in this case, the Relative Range decreases from 5 to 4; this is called Natural Flanking Fire) or flanking occurs when an 'adjacent' friendly group plays a Movement-Flank card sideways and announces the intent to flank  an enemy group.
b. No. When Wire is placed on the flanking group, the flanking advantage is immediately lost until re-established through additional movement.
c. Yes, through the play of another Movement-Flank card or forward Movement to naturally flank. In all cases, once the flanking advantage is lost, it can only be re-acquired through additional Movement.
d. For natural flanking fire, yes. Again natural flanking fire only occurs when two 'adjacent' groups have closed to RR5 and then one of the groups moves forward, passing the other group. For example. We both have groups A and B. My A is at RR1, B at RR3; your A at RR2, B at RR0. If my B moves forward to RR4, that group has naturally flanked your A (we've gone from RR5 to RR4. If your A goes backward, my flank advantage is lost the moment you play your Movement card. I can either move forward for another natural flank, or I could use a Movement-Flank played sideways to flank again. Note that natural flanking fire will only occur at RR4, whereas with a Movement-Flank card, you can achieve a flanking advantage at RR5.

6. Is flanking fire from a card removed by the same methods that you would remove natural flanking fire?
Yes. To re-establish natural flanking fire, you'd have to 'come back' and then 'pass' the targeted group again: natural flanking fire only occurs with the movement action 'past' an enemy group. Once you've passed an enemy group, you are not always entitled to the flanking advantage.

7. To encircle, you have to play a sideways movement card on the flanking group, correct?
Yes, and while still at RR4.

8. Can an encircling group(the one previously flanking) become encircled as well?
Yes.

9. It seems encircling is a much more secure form of flanking because you are able to move and keep encirclement and as long as both groups stay alive or aren't infiltrated, you keep the bonuses, correct?
In theory, yes, but it is quite a task to get to RR5 and then 'past' an enemy group in order to qualify for encirclement. Most flanking will occur with the use of Movement-Flank cards (which can be effective at any range).

ground_truth_answer:
Retreating should be done to prevent flanking and encirclement, which will be addressed in part 2 of the rules.  Vehicles and PC's should retreat if they are getting blown to bits.  Retreating also helps prevent infiltration.  

And yes, that is correct, you can never get to Range 4 if an opposing group is at Range 2 or greater (exception: AFV overruns).  Therefore, you must destroy the opposing group, or at least make them retreat to obtain a higher range chit.  The game gets MUCH more interesting when flanking, encirclement, infiltration and close combat rules come into play.  And after that, you get to look forward to ordnance and AFV's.....even better!!

Moving men from one group to another will be addressed under the Individual Transfer Rules.  That is a risky move because it puts your transferring PC(s) in a very vulnerable position for at least one turn.

Note that the second Stop point in the rules requires that you play the first scenario again, but with these new rules.  I would still play the 1st scenario with the limited rules, just to get a feel for the basics of the game.  When you play it with the second level of rules, even though you are still playing the 1st scenario, I am sure it will be a more enjoyable, rewarding experience

query:
Simplifying Relative Range: I've recently obtained a copy of Up Front, and after many an evening attempting to muddle through the rules, I've reached a "eureka!" moment.

Relative range is given as an abstract concept which causes all dependent factors to be somewhat confusing.  I've come up with what I think is a functionally identical method of showing RR which also makes a lot of other concepts in the game more intuitive:

Picture the groups on a 7xN group, where N is the number of groups, like so:

Point-blank (directly adjacent) is RR 5.  Subtract 1 for each empty space between the two groups.  Diagonal counts as adjacent.  Only count the distance between the groups' rows, not their columns.  Subtract 1 for non-adjacent columns, regardless of distance.

Now things like flanking become much clearer, as it becomes far more obvious when a group is surrounded, or has multiple groups which can fire upon it.  Natural flanking becomes obvious.

As for implementation, I'm printing this board out in the form of 1x7 space strips.  Thoughts are welcome.

I'm excited for more but the learning curve on this one is mighty steep (granted, I'm a wargame newbie). One question came up that I couldn't quite figure out. My group A moved past my opponents group B (relative range went from 5 to 4) putting me in natural flank position on his group B (and vice versa?). He then played two fire cards with double the firepower per the flank advantage and decimated my squad. He played this from a marsh terrain card. Is this legit? The rules give me the impression that a flank position is driven by a movement card. Can someone shed some light on this one for me. Thanks in advance.

Flanking is pretty complicated.  Probably the most complicated rule--until you get to AFV's and anti-tank weapons.

First, in order to flank an opposing group, you MUST have a directly opposing group (i.e. the same letter) to the group you are intending to flank AND EITHER
1)  An adjacent group (i.e. one letter higher or lower) plays a FLANK movement card in sideways mode.  (Lateral Flanking) 
2)  or advancing an adjacent group from RR5 to (what would be) RR6.  (I know it gets converted to RR4.)  (Natural Flanking)
3)  or when your opponent advances an adjacent group from RR5 to RR6.

Situations 2 & 3 can be simultaneous--which seems to be the situation you are describing.  So yes you could both groups flanking each other.

It looks something like this:

         ---> A RC3      RC0 A
B RC0    RC3 B  

Black group has just moved forward from RC2 to RC3.  Black's group A now has flanked Red Group B  (Black has a group B & advaced from RR5 to RR6).  And Red Group B also flanks Black Group A for the same reason.

By the way I positioned the text, it should be clear for the reason for natural flanking.  The group has opposing groups both "in front" and "behind" it.

If say Black had no group B, then Black Group A would not receive flank fire when it advanced, but Red Group B would! 

Play of the movement card allows placement of a Flank Fire chit immediately.  (If two possible groups could be flanked, the flank chit must go on one group or the other, not both.)  While a flank fire chit is in play, the flanking group's firepower is doubled on the flanked group only.  The chit is removed in these situations:

-  The flanking group has a movement card played upon it, even to remove wire.
-  The flanked group has a movement card played upon it (even to remove wire or attempt to ford a stream.)
-  The flanked group has a terrain played up on it.
-  The flanking group rejects terrain played on them by the opponent.  (This would also cause removal/rotation to sideways mode of the movement card used to create the flank. )
-  Elimination or lateral movement away of either the flanking group or the "directly opposite group" required for flanking.

While the movement card the caused the flanking situation is in play the effect of both flanking and movement are in effect and they usually would cancel each other out.  But note that if the flanking group does NOT lose the Flanking chit if they have terrain played on them (either play the player or by the opponent)--so generally you play terrain (any type of terrain, even Marsh (usually you choose something better)) on a flanking group to eliminate the movement card effects on firing.

The key point to remember about flanking:
-  First you place the chit via either a FLANK Movement card in sideways mode or "Natural Flanking" IF you have directly opposing group to group you are trying to flank.
-  So long as the CHIT is present the flanking group doubles its firepower on the flanked group.  But get into good terrain first.

ground_truth_answer:
Actually that Relative Range link isn't dead, it just brings you to wargame designer Mike Nagel's (very interesting!) home page... but here's a direct link to the Relative Range archive (which I got to via Mike Nagel's  relativerange.com page>snippets>upfront in case the link below goes dead). 

http://media.wix.com/ugd/7c7ebf_d9d0f815ed9c4544811dc1391eb83d8a.pdf

Nagel's solitaire system is in essence a simple flowchart of cardplay decisions for the ghost opponent (the live player plays normally), who should be assigned the defensive side of a scenario. Changes to the basic game have been kept to a minimum. There are some restrictions on what terrain can be played and one (smart!) rules change: The ghost-opp makes an automatic die roll for concealment bonus against fire attack; the ghost hand's actual concealment cards are treated as cower cards. The solitaire system does not appear to include a means for the ghostside to attempt infiltration or CC. (*edit -- actually, CC against a vehicle is included in the defenses decision tree.)
